text:
JINAN, China, Aug. 29, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Niutech Technology Group Co., Ltd (abbreviated as "Niutech"), a STAR Market-listed Chinese company specialized in industrial continuous pyrolysis technology, today announced it has signed a sales agreement with a global energy major for an Industrial Continuous Waste Plastic Pyrolysis Production Line. The line runs on Niutech's proprietary patented pyrolysis technology and delivers safe, environmentally sound operation with a single-unit processing capacity of 10,000 to 50,000 tons per year (tpy). The agreement marks Niutech's first entry into the customer's equipment supply chain and the start of a long-term partnership.

As part of its sustainability commitments, the customer has steadily expanded investment in renewable energy in recent years and made Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF) a strategic priority. Under the agreement, Niutech's technology and equipment will be deployed to upgrade a large refinery owned by the customer. Once complete, the refinery will have an integrated capability from pyrolysis oil to hydrotreated SAF.

SAF is widely regarded as a key pathway for aviation decarbonization. Under the EU's ReFuelEU Aviation regulation, SAF blending in jet fuel is mandatory at 2% from 2025, rising to 6% by 2030 and 70% by 2050, while the UK and Singapore have enacted their own blending mandates. Used cooking oil (UCO) is currently the dominant feedstock for SAF production, but limited UCO supply has left the market in urgent need of alternatives. Through Niutech's patented technology, waste plastics can be converted into pyrolysis oil suitable for SAF production, making the feedstock route a promising second option.

Niutech's industrial continuous waste plastic line is highly tolerant of feedstock quality: it requires no complex washing, sorting, drying or fine shredding, and directly pyrolyzes low-value waste plastics — including PP, PE, PS, ABS and nylon, single or mixed — with high efficiency and long-cycle, safe, stable continuous operation at large throughput. Niutech's waste plastic pyrolysis solutions have been commercialized in the UK, South Korea, Denmark, Thailand, Vietnam, China and other markets, supporting multiple 10,000-tonne-scale continuous projects, including the European Waste Plastic Pyrolysis Chemical Recycling Demonstration Project, the Southeast Asian Waste Plastic Pyrolysis Chemical Recycling Demonstration Project, and China's first large-scale continuous pyrolysis project for medical waste plastics.

Waste plastic pyrolysis oil, once an alternative energy source, is now becoming a key upstream feedstock for aviation decarbonization. "Large-scale pyrolysis projects place demanding requirements on the continuous operation capability of the equipment," said a market executive at Niutech. "Niutech has focused on pyrolysis technology for nearly 40 years and brings mature equipment and extensive project experience. This partnership is another validation of the strength of our industrial continuous technology."

About Niutech

Niutech Technology Group Co., Ltd (Stock Code: 688309) is a pyrolysis solutions provider with fully proprietary, globally leading pyrolysis technology, integrating R&D and application, high-end equipment manufacturing and sales, and its own industrial project construction and operation. Its independently developed industrial continuous pyrolysis equipment, with a single-unit processing capacity of 10,000 to 50,000 tpy, has been applied to the disposal of more than 30 waste types, including scrap tires, waste plastics, oily sludge, tar residue, medical waste and biomass. Niutech has helped customers complete 10,000-tonne-scale continuous pyrolysis projects across dozens of countries, including Germany, the UK, South Korea, Denmark and Brazil.

text:
We're working towards net zero carbon emissions from jet fuel by 2050.

Like all airlines, Air New Zealand's business model currently relies on fossil jet fuel, so we're a large emitter of greenhouse gases, including carbon dioxide (CO₂) and other equivalent gases (CO₂-e).

Each year we produce an Annual Report and a Climate Statement (that includes our 2030 Emissions Guidance) to support this approach. You can also read our Transition Plan to net zero carbon emissions from jet fuel by 2050.

Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF) is our most important lever to reduce aviation emissions. It is available today, works in current aircraft and infrastructure, and is certified and safe to use. Our other key decarbonisation levers are:

Fleet and network

Operational efficiency

Carbon credits

Climate Statement

Aotearoa New Zealand relies on aviation for trade, tourism and connectivity. However, both our airline and the sector overall will face climate-related risks as we transition to a low emissions, climate resilient economy.

Air New Zealand publishes a Climate Statement each year in August, with the airline publishing its first Climate Statement in 2024, as required by the Aotearoa New Zealand Climate Standards (NZ CS), structured around the four mandatory sections of the NZ CS. Prior to the introduction of the NZ CS, Air New Zealand voluntarily reported against the Task Force for Climate-related Financial Disclosures (TCFD) framework - from the 2020 financial year.

2030 Emissions Guidance

Air New Zealand also publishes annual 2030 Emissions Guidance, which aims to provide a regular and transparent assessment of the airline’s expected net emissions in 2030.

We aim to design, buy and use products and resources that support the circular economy, and actively work to reduce waste.

As an airline, we use a wide range of materials across our operations that create waste. Exploring ways to rethink what we buy, how we use it, and opportunities to reuse and repurpose materials is a key focus for Air New Zealand.

View our 2026 Annual Report, and our waste targets to find out more.

Our new uniform includes materials such as organic cotton for men's shirts, a recycled polyester and wool blend for the suiting, and recycled polyester for women's dresses and shirts. As our current uniform phases out, we are exploring onshore and offshore recycling options and working on circular solutions when uniforms reach their natural end-of-life through wear and tear as well. One programme we're trialling recycles uniforms into reusable signage, acoustic panels and packaging, with further circular innovations to come as they become viable.

We're focused on reducing waste and improving diversion from landfill. That's why we're exploring recycling options and circular solutions for our current uniforms as they're replaced by new designs from Emilia Wickstead.

We help restore and regenerate nature in Aotearoa New Zealand.

We're the national partner of the 'paw-some' Conservation Dogs Programme as part of our long-standing partnership with the Department of Conservation (DOC). Together with DOC, we also support more than 40,000 hectares of sustained predator control alongside five Great Walks, and the Bats Beyond Borders programme, advancing research and conservation management of New Zealand's threatened native long-tailed bats. One of the most treasured parts of our DOC partnership is the role we play as the airline of choice for some of New Zealand's most threatened species.

We're proud to partner with Trees That Count to support native forest restoration, biodiversity and resilience in Aotearoa New Zealand through our Voluntary Emissions Contribution Programme. To date, Air New Zealand customers have funded more than 500,000 native trees across more than 50 nature, biodiversity and restoration projects.

Air New Zealand's Climate and Nature Fund is funded by an internal carbon charge on select ultra long-haul flights, plus any profits from our loyalty partnership with Z Energy. In the 2026 financial year, the Climate and Nature Fund raised $7.4m, and funded initiatives including supporting two potential domestic SAF projects with Seadra and LanzaJet, the lease costs of the BETA ALIA CX300 electric aircraft, supporting hydrogen fuel cell testing at our Auckland Airport campus, Department of Conservation (DOC) biodiversity projects, the PRISMSS Restoring Island Resilience Awards, and SAF costs.

We're proud to help fly endangered wildlife like the kākāpō across Aotearoa New Zealand through our partnership with the Department of Conservation.

text:
With help from Noah Baustin, Camille von Kaenel and Marisa Guerra Echeverria

MONEY TALKS: President Donald Trump is forcing California leaders to rethink how they’ve designed air quality regulations for half a century.

Craig Segall wants Democrats to open up their wallets.

Segall, a former California Air Resources Board deputy executive officer who is now a policy consultant, helped design the state’s tough emissions standards that would have forced truck manufacturers to sell more electric models.

But that rule is among more than half a dozen policies that congressional Republicans have already killed, or are in the process of revoking.

The Trump administration’s use of the Congressional Review Act — a 1996 law that gives Congress the power to revoke agency rules — to target the EPA has sparked fear that the status quo of California developing its own regulations is “pretty close to irreparably damaged.”

That’s because Republicans are, for the first time in history, using the CRA to roll back EPA waivers that give California the authority to enforce its stricter emissions standards, a tool state officials have used for nearly 60 years to address its uniquely poor air quality.

Segall spoke with POLITICO about Republicans’ attacks on California’s climate and pollution goals, and how he thinks Democrats in California and D.C. should respond.

This transcript has been edited for length and clarity.

Have Republicans fundamentally undermined California’s ability to enforce stricter emissions standards and reach its climate goals?

They are. Let’s start with what’s happening. There’s no way at all for California to meaningfully comply with basic public health requirements, much less climate targets, if it can’t regulate heavy-duty vehicles. So this is an important set of attacks, given that they’re both against new on-road vehicles and off-road vehicles. The whole swath of this is functionally making it almost impossible to do anything about either traditional cars and trucks, but also things like ships that are driving a huge amount of cancer and asthma.

I think the easy way to understand this is if [Republicans] don’t have the votes to repeal the California waiver authorization programs, you could do so functionally by breaking the law, and using this tactic to the point where there’s fundamentally almost not usable provisions without large amounts of legal risk. Even they probably don’t have the votes to repeal the filibuster for a substantive amendment to [the Clean Air Act]. So what you wind up with is this very weird, procedural workaround that does the same thing.

What do you think Democrats should do about it?

I think a few things are clear. One is that the existing structure is pretty close to irreparably damaged. So even in a world in which Democrats run the table, at this point you’re talking about well into the 2030s before any new rules could even take effect. And it’s unclear that there would be the political consensus under current conditions to implement them. Because as long as it’s true that any regulation you put a lot of effort into can be “CRA’d” out of existence by this waiver authorization workaround, those regulations are going to be very hard to get good compliance with.

So the real question is: How do you get a political consensus going on a new path here? It speaks to the need for industrial and economic policy approaches. We do know what it looks like when countries sprint to electrification. It looks a lot like East Asia, and that looks like a success. The next governor and the next president will come in with the air quality-based system that we’ve had for 50 years pretty badly broken. They will also face ongoing high gas and diesel prices and a U.S. industrial base that’s way behind its competitors. And the question is, what deal can you forge?

Maybe we wind up with a national program that’s much more focused on supporting areas of electrification in which we still have a comparative advantage. Maybe it’s market access and joint ventures. Parts of the [Inflation Reduction Act] that survived, right? That is a pretty good test of it. Congress likes supporting manufacturing of zero-emission vehicles and batteries. I think we’re likely to see the end of this EV political winter, just given what’s happened to oil and gas prices. Then Congress is going to like cheap and affordable EVs, and it’s going to want to meet here.

Lawn care equipment is already partially electrifying all over the world, largely because landscapers don’t like being poisoned by fumes and don’t like paying for diesel either. So you can imagine a package that looks like a mix of industrial policy, affordability policy, and yeah, probably some pushing on the manufacturers that gets you much of the way there.

Are you describing a policy platform that looks like President Joe Biden’s, which invested billions in clean energy and climate change programs?

The Biden strategy was still very strongly regulatory through EPA, but we’ve seen that the parts that were bipartisan — manufacturing — survived.

So there will be elements of Biden, but I think there need to be real catch-up policies, and that probably includes some conversations around what we ask manufacturers to do. Biden never hard-coded manufacturing targets, which is a problem. At the same time, [California] needs to find room fiscally and structurally to get there. There’s a lot you can do here using state finances, tax policy, and industrial policy to keep it moving. You can hypothesize about regulations that should be passed, but those regulations will not move the substantive needle because they can’t be implemented. So your base strategy has to instead be: How do you deploy large amounts of really affordable EVs, and build as much as possible with a supply chain that’s onshored and therefore provides wage support.

What sort of signals do you want to see from a likely future Becerra administration?

I would say, recognize that they have room to move. What we want to see is a path that really doubles down on making it genuinely affordable for people and helping build the whole supply chain here. Here, being both California and the U.S. That’s where there’s momentum. I just think with a governor coming in who is someone really committed to economic equality, somebody who’s committed to using all the tools of government, as he seems to be, there’s this chance to get creative, and to me, that seems like the really important thing. That there’s room to genuinely be creative with the government’s spending powers, and learn from the experience we’ve had. That that’s what’s valuable. Not either intransigence or folding, but instead sort of announcing and finding the ways that will really work in this setting.

BEGINNING OF THE END: Happy 72-hour rule day, for those who celebrate.

For those uninitiated in the wiles of Sacramento, that’s a reference to the constitutional requirement that lawmakers must put bill amendments into print at least 72 hours before the Legislature passes them. With the session ending Monday, that makes Friday night the time to finalize any deals.

Gov. Gavin Newsom’s much discussed proposal to reshape who pays after utilities cause wildfires had not made it into bill form by press time. But the governor’s plan was at serious risk as of Friday morning.

While talks continued between Newsom’s office and lawmakers, the most controversial and transformative elements of the governor’s proposal will not be in a final deal, barring a late-hour turnaround, two people familiar with the negotiations who were granted anonymity to discuss the private talks told POLITICO. Stock prices for Pacific Gas & Electric, Edison International and Sempra Energy dropped after the news came out.

Those elements that lawmakers appear unwilling to budge on in Newsom’s proposal include: stopping insurance companies from recouping their losses from utilities after wildfires, capping emotional distress claims for uninjured people who were within the perimeter of fire danger and barring local governments and corporations from recovering the full replacement cost of damaged infrastructure from utilities.

On Friday afternoon, the governor’s office said that Newsom’s team had passed an offer back to the Legislature to address lawmakers’ concerns over eliminating subrogation. Despite the sources saying the issue was not going to be part of the final deal, Newsom’s team said conversations remain ongoing, and that they are continuing to negotiate with the intent to address broader structural concerns. Noah’s got the full breakdown for subscribers.

ON THE GOVERNOR’S DESK: More bills are heading Newsom’s way. Here are a handful on our radars.

SB 894, by Sen. Ben Allen, would set up state-backed loans for fire-resistant home retrofits. The measure is one of the first bills caught up in broader wildfire liability talks to make it out of the Legislature; it’s part of the Senate’s overall wildfire package, and was also listed in one of the governor’s office’s opening memos in the talks.

SB 954, by Sen. Catherine Blakespear, would bolster environmental review requirements for some advanced manufacturing facilities. A priority bill for environmentalists still smarting from the Legislature’s rollbacks to environmental reviews last year, it advanced despite significant opposition from business and manufacturing groups, who are already pressuring Newsom to veto (read more in our story for subscribers).

AB 40, by Assemblymember Mia Bonta, would add more environmental review hurdles for coal handling and export projects around the state. That measure emerged as a direct response to the Trump administration’s announcement in June that it was investing $75 million in a controversial project to build a coal export facility in Oakland.

AB 1448, by Assemblymember Gregg Hart, would prohibit the use of existing oil and gas infrastructure located in California coastal territory from being used to support federal offshore oil leases issued after Jan. 1, 2026. That would make it effectively impossible to transport oil from a newly-leased federal territory to shore via a pipeline.

AB 2313, by Assemblymember Marc Berman, would set up a program in which natural gas providers must offer residents whose service lines need replacing the option to instead accept an incentive to cut their gas service, bolstering electrification.

FLIGHT PATH: Opponents of a proposed tax credit for sustainable aviation fuel are quoting the company that would benefit most in their pitch to lawmakers to reject it.

Newsom’s office is pushing a proposal that would allow fuel producers to reduce their diesel tax payments in exchange for refining more non-petroleum jet fuel, a concept his finance officials have said would help clean up the aviation sector. Market analysts believe the tax credit would largely benefit Phillips 66’s refinery in the Bay Area city of Rodeo, the largest producer of renewable diesel and sustainable aviation fuel refined from plant and animal-based oils.

Supporters, including a bipartisan group of lawmakers, argue the credit is needed to prop up a facility that had reported hundreds of millions in losses since becoming fully operational in 2024. But the opposition, which includes local government, construction unions and the California Fuels and Convenience Alliance, argues the finances no longer pencil out.

Those groups circulated a flyer around the Capitol on Friday that points to the fact that the Rodeo refinery reported $544 million in profits between April and June, and quotes Phillips 66 CEO Mark Lashier’s statement from a June conference that the facility is “running extraordinarily well.”

Concerns about the aviation fuel credit have largely centered on projections that it could reduce renewable diesel production — raising pump prices and lowering diesel tax revenues that support transportation projects. Newsom’s office and P66 have countered that those fears are overblown.

The tax credit hadn’t been introduced in a bill as of press time. — AN

WHERE THERE’S SMOKE: Wildfire survivors are raising alarm bells about last-minute negotiations over a pair of bills that would set first-in-the-nation standards for insurance claims for contamination from wildfire smoke.

Assemblymembers John Harabedian and Mike Gipson are in the thick of negotiations over their dueling bills on the issue, AB 1642 and AB 1795, respectively, according to three sources close to the negotiations who did not want to be named because of the fluidity of the situation.

The insurance industry has opposed the bills because of costs, and the governor’s office has also sent recommendations in recent days, according to emails obtained by POLITICO.

Jane Lawton Potelle, executive director of Eaton Fire Residents United, the sponsor of Harabedian’s bill, warned against any changes that could narrow who could bring claims under the new standards.

“Insurers must remain obligated to return homes to pre-loss condition using science-based standards for human habitability, regardless of their homes’ location,” Lawton Potelle said in a statement to POLITICO. “The standards set in AB 1642 should apply to everyone with wildfire smoke damage.”

As of press time, no amendments had made it into print yet.

As of press time, no amendments had made it into print yet. Harabedian called his bill “first in the nation legislation that will provide unprecedented protections for wildfire survivors” in a statement to POLITICO on Friday afternoon. — CvK

HEADWINDS: California’s big offshore wind lawsuit is officially here.

Attorney General Rob Bonta and the California Energy Commission announced a new lawsuit against the Trump administration on Friday challenging the cancellation of Golden State Wind off the central California coast, Niina H. Farah reports for subscribers. The case was filed in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California.

The Interior Department revealed in April that it had agreed to pay Golden State Wind $120 million to abandon its project and invest instead in fossil fuel projects. The loss of the 2-gigawatt offshore project, which would have provided enough clean electricity to power more than 1 million homes, also means California will no longer receive more than $30 million in workforce development and other funds to local communities, the lawsuit says.

“Make no mistake, California won’t stand idly by while the Trump administration uses and abuses taxpayer dollars to dismantle an industry we’ve spent years building,” Bonta said during a press conference Friday. — CvK

In addition, R&D World magazine named ORNL's Parans Paranthaman its 2026 Researcher of the Year , recognizing his work in materials science, energy technology and advanced manufacturing.

"ORNL continues to lead in delivering innovative technologies that move science from the laboratory into real-world impact," said ORNL Director Stephen Streiffer. "This year's R&D 100 Awards highlight our strengths across energy, manufacturing, computing and biotechnology, as well as the value of our partnerships in advancing solutions that benefit the nation."

ORNL's 2026 R&D 100 Award winners

Affordable Efficient Thermoelectric Dishwasher with Enhanced Drying - Developed with Samsung Electronics America, the dishwasher uses a solid-state heat pump and wastewater heat recovery to reduce energy consumption while improving drying performance.

AWARE: Multi-Event Grid Intelligence Platform for Wildfire Prevention and Resilience - Developed with Southern California Edison, the AI-enhanced platform detects and classifies abnormal power grid conditions that can contribute to wildfires, equipment damage and blackouts.

GeoWISE: Geothermal Heat Pump Web-Based Integrated Simulation and Economic Analysis Tool - Developed with Oklahoma State University, the web-based platform rapidly evaluates geothermal feasibility for buildings, campuses and communities by automating energy modeling, simulations and infrastructure sizing.

Microgrid Orchestrator: A Distributed Controller for Networked Microgrids - Developed with New Sun Road and Casa Pueblo, the technology coordinates electricity transfers among connected microgrids to improve reliability and resilience while reducing costs.

Multiplexing Extrusion System (MExS) - Developed with the University of Maine, the additive manufacturing system can simultaneously deposit multiple materials within a single printed bead, doubling deposition throughput while enabling new combinations of structural and functional materials.

ORNL & BMW 22kW Polyphase Wireless Power Transfer System with Rotating Magnetic Fields - Developed with BMW Group, the compact wireless vehicle charging system delivers twice the charging power of current standard wireless systems while occupying 61 percent less space and maintaining more than 95 percent charging efficiency.

PASTREE: Phosphoric Acid Sludge Treatment for Rare Earths Extraction - Developed with the Florida Industrial and Phosphate Research Institute, PASTREE streamlines the recovery of rare earth elements and other valuable materials from phosphate industry by-products, reducing capital and operating costs while providing a more economically viable recovery pathway.

Recycled Composite Oven - Developed with Whirlpool Corporation, the residential oven replaces a traditional steel cavity with fiberglass composites and thermoset polymers to reduce energy demand while maintaining cooking performance.

Terpenes Conversion to Aviation Fuel - Developed with Captis Aire, the technology converts waste terpenes from the wood industry into hydrocarbons that can be blended into sustainable aviation fuel.

Programmable Tri-Structural Isotropic (TRISO) Nuclear Fuel - Developed by ORNL with TRISO-X and Arc Impact, the technology precisely controls the placement of TRISO fuel particles rather than relying on random packing, increasing fuel density and potentially extending fuel cycles.

Electrochemical CO2 Graphitization (ECOG) - The process converts carbon dioxide directly into high-purity graphitic carbon at 550 degrees Celsius, far below the temperatures required for conventional graphite manufacturing, offering a less energy-intensive pathway to battery-grade graphite.

MS-PolyFuel Technology - ORNL researchers developed MS-PolyFuel Technology, a molten-salt system that converts waste polyethylene and other polymers into gasoline- and diesel-range hydrocarbons under mild conditions. The technology uses inexpensive, recyclable salts as both solvent and catalyst, eliminating the need for noble-metal catalysts, organic solvents or external hydrogen.

NEAREST: Neutral Extractant Advanced Rare Earth Separation Technology - The technology uses a new two-ligand approach to separate individual rare earth elements while reducing chemical use, waste and projected processing costs compared with conventional methods.

Algae Composite - Developed with the California Institute of Technology, the low-cost composite uses wastewater algae and agricultural residues to produce material for applications such as lightweight structural panels, packaging and insulation.

Thermophilic One-Pot Bioconversion of PET Waste into Value-Added Aromatics - Developed with the National Laboratory of the Rockies, the process uses an engineered heat-loving microbe to convert polyethylene terephthalate (PET) plastic waste into a higher-value industrial chemical in a single step.

tSAGE: Thermostable Serine Recombinase Assisted Genome Engineering - This biotechnology platform reduces the time required to add new DNA to heat-loving industrial microbes from about four weeks to about three days, enabling rapid development of biotechnologies for high-temperature manufacturing.

ATLAS-Tx - ATLAS-Tx, an AI technology developed by ORNL and the National Institute of Environmental Health Sciences, predicts gene activity in hard-to-access tissues using data from tissues that are easier to sample.

LuGo: An Enhanced Quantum Phase Estimation Implementation - ORNL developed LuGo, a software framework that makes quantum computing faster and more efficient. LuGo improves a core quantum algorithm by generating circuits more than 50 times faster and reducing quantum gates and circuit depth by more than 30-fold without sacrificing accuracy.

ORNL also contributed to four winning technologies led by partner institutions:

Persistent DynAMICS - Led by Los Alamos National Laboratory with ORNL and other partner organizations, Persistent DynAMICS is a lightweight software platform that enables distributed sensing systems to operate as a unified, responsive network. It integrates with existing sensors, data systems and processing tools as an overlay without requiring hardware replacement or increasing user burden.

Pulsar-Based Timing System: An Alternative Time Reference for Resilient Synchronization - Led by the University of Tennessee, Knoxville, with ORNL, the system uses radio signals from rotating neutron stars, or pulsars, to provide a resilient timing reference for power grid applications when satellite-based timing is disrupted.

Pele Suite of Exascale Reacting Flow Codes - The National Laboratory of the Rockies developed Pele in collaboration with ORNL and other national laboratory partners. The open-source simulation software suite uses exascale computing to model complex turbulent reacting flows found in energy, transportation, manufacturing and other applications.

Tritium Migration Analysis Program: TMAP8 - Led by Idaho National Laboratory with ORNL, the open-source computational tool models tritium movement and fuel cycle technologies in fusion energy systems, in which effective tritium management is critical to safety, sustainability and economic viability.

title: Coconut oil could offer airlines another path toward alternative jet fuel
description:
Coconut oil can be turned into biofuel that runs in a small jet engine when blended with conventional jet fuel.
Coconut oil may seem far removed from a jet engine, but its chemistry gives it an unusual advantage.
Coconut oil stands out because its fatty acid chain lengths are similar to the hydrocarbon chain lengths needed for jet fuel.
Dig deeper into sustainable aviation fuel and jet engine emissions These resources examine coconut-derived turbine fuels, sustainable aviation fuel performance, life-cycle emissions and the technical challenges involved in replacing conventional jet fuel.
The original story "Coconut oil could offer airlines another path toward alternative jet fuel" is published in The Brighter Side of News.
text:
Coconut oil can be turned into biofuel that runs in a small jet engine when blended with conventional jet fuel.

The blends kept engine efficiency close to standard Jet A-1 and reduced hydrocarbon emissions, but fuel consumption increased.

The fuel could be useful in coconut-producing regions, though storage stability, material compatibility and full environmental impacts still need study.

Coconut oil may seem far removed from a jet engine, but its chemistry gives it an unusual advantage. Its fatty acid chains are close in length to the hydrocarbons used in aviation fuel.

A team from Osaka Metropolitan University has now tested coconut oil-based biofuels in a small turbojet engine. The work focused on whether these fuels could be blended with Jet A-1, a conventional aviation fuel, without reducing engine performance.

The researchers made two biofuels from coconut oil. One, called FAME, used methanol. The other, called FAEE, used ethanol. Both were produced through a co-solvent method that combines coconut oil extracts with acetone and alcohol.

The method works under ambient temperature and pressure. That could reduce energy consumption during production while helping preserve fuel purity.

A cleaner fuel search with strict demands

Airlines and consumers have become increasingly concerned about carbon, nitrogen and hydrocarbon emissions. Biofuels have drawn attention as one possible greener alternative.

Aviation fuel has a difficult job. It must deliver high energy in a compact form. It also has to work safely in existing engines across demanding conditions.

Coconut oil stands out because its fatty acid chain lengths are similar to the hydrocarbon chain lengths needed for jet fuel. That means it could require less processing than some other plant oils before use in aviation fuel blends.

The Osaka Metropolitan University team tested different blend ratios of FAME and FAEE with Jet A-1. Their goal was to find a balance among fuel consumption, thermal efficiency and exhaust gas emissions.

The researchers used a small turbojet engine for the trials. That allowed them to compare performance and emissions under controlled conditions.

Efficiency held steady, fuel use rose

The tests showed a trade-off. As the biofuel blending ratio increased, fuel consumption also increased.

The likely reason was the difference in heating value between the biofuels and Jet A-1. Heating value describes how much energy a fuel releases when burned. If a fuel releases less energy per unit, an engine may need more of it to produce the same output.

Even so, thermal efficiency remained comparable to Jet A-1. Thermal efficiency measures how well an engine turns fuel energy into useful work.

That result matters because a potential biofuel cannot simply burn. It must run in current engine systems without major loss of performance.

“The experiments showed that our fuel blend can operate in existing gas turbine engines without major loss of efficiency or engine performance, and without increasing emissions,” Dr. Huynh Phuong Uyen Nguyen of the Graduate School of Sustainable System Sciences summarized.

The study did not show that coconut biofuel can fully replace conventional jet fuel. The tested fuels were blends with Jet A-1. The researchers also identified fuel consumption as a target for improvement.

Exhaust results showed a mixed picture

The biofuel blends reduced hydrocarbon emissions. Hydrocarbons in exhaust can come from unburned or partly burned fuel.

That decrease is one of the stronger practical signs from the engine trials. It suggests that adding coconut oil-derived fuel can change the exhaust profile in a favorable way for at least one pollutant category.

The team also found no significant changes in carbon dioxide or nitric oxide emissions. Those pollutants are central to the carbon and nitrogen footprints of airlines.

The result does not mean the fuel has no climate or environmental impact. Carbon dioxide from combustion is only one part of the full picture. Production, transport and storage also matter.

That is why the researchers plan to assess environmental impacts through life cycle assessment. Such an analysis would examine the broader footprint of producing and using the fuel.

A fuel source in discarded coconuts

The findings could be especially relevant for Asian countries, including those in Southeast Asia. The region grows large numbers of coconuts and also faces fuel-security concerns.

About 30 percent of harvested coconuts in Southeast Asia are discarded because they do not meet commercial standards. That discarded material could become a feedstock for biofuel production.

Using rejected coconuts would avoid relying only on higher-value commercial products. It could also create a local resource for countries at risk of fuel shock.

The study’s production method may also fit that regional context. Because the co-solvent method operates under ambient temperature and pressure, it may need less energy than more intensive processing routes.

Still, scaling from laboratory and engine testing to practical aviation use would require further development. Fuel quality must remain stable over time. It must also be compatible with engine materials and storage systems.

Beyond blends toward future engines

The research team sees several next steps. One is improving fuel consumption performance. Another is establishing technologies for operating engines on 100 percent biofuel.

“In the future, we want to improve fuel consumption performance and establish technologies for operating engines on 100% biofuel,” Dr. Ogawa said.

That is an ambitious target. The current work supports blended use, not full replacement. But the engine results provide a starting point for further testing.

Ogawa also pointed to practical barriers beyond engine operation.

“Looking ahead, we also want to advance the practical application of this fuel by improving its long-term storage stability, material compatibility, and environmental impacts through life cycle assessment.”

Those issues are not minor. Aviation fuels must remain safe and reliable from production through storage, transport and use. A fuel that performs well in an engine test still needs to meet broader durability and safety demands.

Practical implications of the research

The study gives aviation fuel researchers a clearer look at coconut oil-derived biofuel under real engine conditions. It shows that FAME and FAEE blends can run in an existing gas turbine engine without major efficiency loss or emission increases.

That could help guide future work on biofuels made from discarded coconut material, especially in regions where coconuts are abundant and fuel supply risks matter. The reduced hydrocarbon emissions also give researchers a specific performance benefit to investigate further.

The main practical challenge is improving fuel consumption while proving long-term stability, compatibility and environmental value. If those issues can be addressed, coconut oil-based fuels could become one more option in the broader search for lower-impact aviation fuel.

Dig deeper into sustainable aviation fuel and jet engine emissions

These resources examine coconut-derived turbine fuels, sustainable aviation fuel performance, life-cycle emissions and the technical challenges involved in replacing conventional jet fuel.

Development and turbine engine testing of coconut oil-based biojet fuel: Researchers produced high-purity coconut oil ethyl esters and tested blends containing 10% to 30% renewable fuel in a small gas turbine. Engine operation remained stable, although specific fuel consumption increased as the coconut-derived fraction rose. (Fuel Processing Technology, 2025)

Overview of combustion and emission characteristics of sustainable aviation fuels and standard JET A-1 fuel: This review compares the physical properties, combustion behavior and emissions of sustainable aviation fuels with conventional Jet A-1. It also examines the technical requirements and remaining challenges for increasing SAF blending levels in aircraft engines. (Fuel, 2025)

The Prospects and Challenges of Sustainable Aviation Fuels (SAFs) for Clean Combustion in Gas Turbine Engines: A Review: This review evaluates SAF combustion, emissions, engine operability and compatibility with existing turbine components. It highlights the engineering challenges that become increasingly important as aviation moves toward higher SAF concentrations. (Energy & Fuels, 2026)

Sustainable aviation fuel from waste cooking Oil: Pathways, Catalysts, and Prospects: This review examines technologies for converting waste oils into aviation fuel, particularly hydroprocessed esters and fatty acids and catalytic hydrothermolysis. It provides broader context for using discarded lipid feedstocks as alternatives to petroleum-derived jet fuel. (Fuel, 2026)

Sustainable aviation fuel pathways: Emissions, costs and uncertainty: This meta-analysis compares greenhouse gas emissions, costs and uncertainty across several major SAF production pathways. It shows why combustion tests alone cannot establish a fuel’s environmental benefits and why full life-cycle assessment remains essential. (Resources, Conservation and Recycling, 2025)

Research findings are available online in the journal Fuel.

text:
Canadian farmers planted a record 23.4 million acres of canola in 2026, according to Statistics Canada. That number tells an important story about the scale of canola in Canadian agriculture. It also points to a less visible fact: every acre depends on strong crop establishment, and seed treatments play a critical role in that success.

Seed treatments are the first line of defence against early-season pests and diseases. In canola, growers rely on fungicide and insecticide seed treatments to protect seedlings during the crop’s most vulnerable stage. Without that protection, even the best genetics can fall short before the crop is fully established.

Innovation in seed treatment technology is driven by what growers face in the field. For Canadian canola growers, two key establishment risks are flea beetles and soil- and seed-borne pathogen complex. These threats can reduce emergence, weaken plant stands, and limit yield potential from the start.

The Bayer SeedGrowth® platform helps advance better canola and manage those risks by combining crop protection innovation with advanced formulation technology. The goal? Seed treatment formulations that deliver reliable seed coverage, accurate active ingredient placement, and consistent performance in real-world conditions.

A defining example is BUTEO® start insecticide seed treatment introduced in 2021, which delivers a non-neonic mode of action for flea beetle management in canola, providing growers with an important tool against persistent early-season threats. Developed to strengthen the protection during the critical emergence and establishment period, its rapid uptake and systemic movement within the plant help deliver reliable performance across a range of growing conditions.

More broadly, this seed treatment demonstrates how canola innovation builds on proven seed treatment foundations, expanding the technologies available to growers while helping protect crop establishment, support sustainable pest management, and give every acre the strongest possible start.

Innovation takes time. Even with faster discovery platforms, it can still take up to 14 years to move a new active ingredient from discovery through development and regulatory review to on-farm use. New formulations built from existing modes of action and mixing partners can move faster, but they may still require 8 to 10 years before they are available to farmers.

Whether canola is grown for food oil, livestock feed, renewable diesel, or sustainable aviation fuel, productivity starts with crop establishment. Robust seed treatments help Canadian growers improve productivity, support sustainability, and protect profitability.

text:
LUBBOCK, TX – High diesel prices are improving the competitive position of biofuels, but sustainable aviation fuel still faces tougher economics than renewable diesel. CoBank lead economist Jacqui Fatka says facilities capable of producing both fuels currently have stronger financial incentives to make renewable diesel.

Sustainable aviation fuel remains more expensive to produce than conventional alternatives, although federal tax incentives can narrow the gap. Recent policy changes also reduced the incentive available for sustainable aviation fuel production.

Many renewable diesel facilities can shift some production toward aviation fuel, giving operators flexibility when market conditions change. For now, Fatka says renewable diesel generally offers the better return.

That matters for agriculture because both fuels can compete for similar feedstocks, including soybean oil, animal fats, and other renewable oils. Production economics can influence where those supplies ultimately move.

Fatka says airlines could increase demand through purchasing commitments, but sustainable aviation fuel currently faces more economic headwinds than tailwinds in the U.S. market.

Farm-Level Takeaway: Renewable diesel currently offers stronger economics than sustainable aviation fuel, shaping competition for agricultural feedstocks.

Pratt & Whitney, an RTX (NYSE: RTX) business, has been awarded a nearly $1.3 billion undefinitized contract for F135 engine spare parts. The F135 powers all three variants of the F-35 Lightning II, the world's most advanced fighter aircraft.

text:
Airport Authority Hong Kong (AAHK) has released its Sustainability Report 2025/26, outlining progress at Hong Kong International Airport (HKG) across environmental, operational, economic and social priorities.

AAHK continues to implement its Ascend sustainability strategy, which is structured around 24 strategic goals across four pillars: Environmental Excellence, Operational Excellence, Thriving Economies and Societies, and Thriving People.

The report highlights the airport’s progress in strengthening environmental resilience and sustainability. HKIA’s Flood Resilience Studies received the highest Platinum award at the Airports Council International Asia-Pacific & Middle East Green Airports Recognition 2026.

For the first time, the report also includes a Nature-related Financial Disclosure Statement, making HKIA one of the first airports in Asia to adopt recommendations from the Taskforce on Nature-related Financial Disclosures.

AAHK has strengthened its double materiality assessment through reviews of the global risk environment, value chain mapping and megatrend analysis. The assessment is designed to identify sustainability-related impacts, risks and opportunities affecting stakeholders and the authority.

Environmental progress

AAHK achieved its target of increasing the airport’s recyclables recovery rate by 25 per cent by 2025 against a 2018 baseline. The authority also completed the deployment and monitoring of 500 additional artificial reef units in North Lantau waters, providing shelter and nursery areas for marine species.

Passenger infrastructure has also been developed. New departure facilities and the Coach Hall at the expanded Terminal 2 were commissioned, increasing capacity while supporting the passenger experience.

AAHK also launched Park & Fly and Park & Visit services. The initiatives use the Hong Kong-Zhuhai-Macao Bridge to provide passengers and visitors with parking facilities connected to HKIA and destinations across Hong Kong.

Digital and operational resilience

Operational resilience remains another focus, with AAHK conducting 36 drills and exercises, including a full-scale passenger departures trial at Terminal 2 and an aircraft crash and rescue exercise.

Phase 2 of the Digital Apron and Tower Management System was substantially completed, with eight additional cameras installed across the Three-runway System to strengthen real-time monitoring, situational awareness and operational planning.

The airport also implemented an Arrival Baggage Tracking System and introduced a real-time visualisation dashboard in Terminal 1 baggage halls to monitor baggage movements from aircraft stands.

AAHK completed the first phase of a human-like customer service avatar powered by generative artificial intelligence, designed to handle passenger enquiries in three languages.

The report also highlights investment in staff development, with more than 94,000 hours of in-person and online training delivered during the year, alongside an enhanced Staff Recognition Programme.

title: Singapore plays by the rules and won't tolerate tariff evasion, says trade minister
description:
The US has accused Chinese exporters of using third countries to disguise the origin of goods to avoid tariffs.
Singapore has rejected the suggestion that its legitimate transhipment trade amounted to tariff evasion.
Goods moving through Singapore remain China-origin goods unless they undergo processing in Singapore that meets applicable rules of origin.
Singapore Customs has reiterated that the US uses the “substantial transformation” test when determining whether a product qualifies as Singapore-origin.
Mr Gan pointed to a recent Singapore enforcement case as evidence that the government was prepared to act against companies that cross that line.
text:
Singapore is making clear that its position as one of Asia’s biggest transhipment and trading hubs does not extend to helping exporters disguise the Chinese origin of goods to circumvent US tariffs.

Deputy PM and trade minister Gan Kim Yong (pictured) said Singapore did not support the use of its trade and logistics infrastructure to bypass tariffs, as the city-state seeks to address US allegations over the rerouting of China-made goods through third countries.

At the Economic Society of Singapore’s 70th anniversary dinner, he said: “We frown upon such practices.”

Mr Gan, recently on a US visit, during which he met with US trade representative Jamieson Greer, emphasised that Singapore must maintain the credibility it had built as a trusted international trading hub.

“It’s important for us to safeguard that trust by making sure that we are very stringent on the rules of origin… From time to time, we do need to take action, to demonstrate our seriousness in enforcing the rules.”

Washington recently identified Singapore as one of around 40 economies allegedly forming part of what it described as a “shadow transhipment network”. The US has accused Chinese exporters of using third countries to disguise the origin of goods to avoid tariffs.

Singapore has rejected the suggestion that its legitimate transhipment trade amounted to tariff evasion. And for Singapore’s maritime and logistics sector, the distinction is critical.

Transhipment does not change a product’s country of origin. Goods moving through Singapore remain China-origin goods unless they undergo processing in Singapore that meets applicable rules of origin.

Singapore Customs has reiterated that the US uses the “substantial transformation” test when determining whether a product qualifies as Singapore-origin. Minimal processing or assembly normally does not confer this status. That means a Chinese-made product cannot simply be shipped into Singapore, repacked or minimally processed, and then declared as Singapore-origin to obtain preferential treatment or avoid US tariffs.

Mr Gan pointed to a recent Singapore enforcement case as evidence that the government was prepared to act against companies that cross that line.

On 14 August, a Singapore-registered company, Healthy Living Biotech, Singapore residents Yin Yuxi, 28, and Bernard Koh Wee Yiap, 54, along with Chinese national Xue Xin, 37, were charged over falsely declared China-made mattresses as Singapore-origin goods to evade US import duties.

text:
EVA Air, AIT Worldwide Logistics and Microsoft have launched a two year programme to promote the use of sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) made from used cooking oil. The initiative is expected to reduce around 15 thsd tons of CO₂ emissions from Microsoft’s supply chain during its first year, UkrAgroConsult reported.

Taiwan’s Formosa Petrochemical will produce the SAF using used cooking oil as the feedstock. Both the raw material and the production process are certified under the ISCC system. The companies said the fuel can reduce lifecycle greenhouse gas emissions by around 80% compared with conventional jet fuel.

Under the programme, EVA Air will provide Microsoft with SAF environmental attributes linked to flights departing from Taiwan. This will enable Microsoft to account for Scope 3 emissions reductions associated with air freight transportation of equipment used for its cloud infrastructure.

The use of SAF is already part of EVA Air’s long term strategy. The airline has been using sustainable aviation fuel on flights departing Asia, Europe and North America since 2025. It has also entered into a five year SAF procurement agreement with Formosa Petrochemical.

The growing use of SAF is also increasing demand for used vegetable oils, which are among the main feedstocks used to produce the fuel through the HEFA pathway. Platts assessed SAF HEFA SPK FOB Straits at $2,487.25 per ton on August 25, down $10 from the previous day.

title: Micro-reactors set to yield 300,000 tons of fuel from methane waste - Interesting Engineering
description:

These systems are designed to convert waste gas directly into liquid fuels without relying on new pipeline or grid infrastructure.

text:
Emvolon, an MIT spinout developing technology to turn methane-rich waste gas into liquid fuels, has signed two commercial agreements with commodities trader Freepoint Commodities to scale production, targeting up to 300,000 metric tons annually as projects are deployed globally.

Under a seven-year commodity purchase agreement, Freepoint will become the primary buyer of biomethanol and other liquid fuels produced at Emvolon’s projects. The fuel will enter Freepoint’s existing physical distribution network, giving Emvolon an established route to market as production expands.

The second agreement gives Freepoint rights to co-invest in Emvolon’s project portfolio through equity and debt. The arrangement is designed to provide capital alongside technology deployment, particularly for projects using waste gas from landfills, dairy farms and industrial sites.

Emvolon, founded in 2021, is developing systems that convert methane-rich waste gases into fuels and chemicals at the location where the waste is generated.

Waste gas becomes fuel

The company’s approach uses modular micro-reactors built around mass-produced automotive engines. These systems are designed to convert waste gas directly into liquid fuels without relying on new pipeline or grid infrastructure.

That could allow fuel production at sites where methane would otherwise be flared, released or left unused. Emvolon says its model can be applied to different feedstocks and locations, reducing the need for bespoke engineering for each project.

More from Energy

See All

“Energy security and supply chain resilience and sustainability dictate that we produce essential liquid fuels locally using domestic waste resources that are currently flared or lost,” said Emmanuel Kasseris, Ph.D., Co-Founder and CEO of Emvolon. “This dual commercial and capital agreement with Freepoint systematically solves the core bottleneck in decentralized fuel manufacturing by securing our buyer and anchoring our project financing platform. We are building our first commercial system now and will put that foundation to work across North America and key international growth regions.”

The companies see methanol as a significant market for the technology. Methanol is used in shipping, heavy transport and chemical production, while newer pathways are also being developed to use methanol in sustainable aviation fuel production.

Emvolon says low-carbon biomethanol that meets RED-II requirements can command a premium of more than $1,000 per metric ton. Its strategy is to produce the commodity close to waste sources, potentially cutting infrastructure requirements and transportation needs.

Capital backs modular rollout

Freepoint’s investment rights could also help Emvolon move individual projects from technology deployment toward long-term financing. Rather than simply licensing its technology, Emvolon plans to package feedstock access, fuel production, financing and product sales into a single project model.

The company has already demonstrated part of this approach through a joint venture with Montauk Renewables, which provides access to waste-gas resources.

“Freepoint is focused on building resilient commodity supply chains and identifying proprietary technologies capable of scaling rapidly to meet physical supply deficits,” said Mark Lay, Managing Director at Freepoint. “Emvolon’s modular deployment model offers a practical solution to localized fuel production. Our dual commercial and capital commitment reflects our commitment to renewable chemicals and fuels.”

The model is intended to support projects across landfill, agricultural and industrial waste streams in North America and other regions. If deployment scales as planned, the 300,000-metric-ton annual target would give the partnership a sizeable position in the emerging market for waste-derived fuels.

title: Opinion: While Washington closes doors, Illinois opens markets for farmers - Agri-Pulse
description:
Illinois farmers did not start President Trump’s trade wars.
Illinois farmers lead the nation in soybean production, supporting jobs and businesses across rural communities while feeding families and industries thousands of miles away.
President Trump’s tariffs and unpredictable trade policies have threatened the export markets Illinois farmers spent generations developing.
But developing new customers helps farmers diversify their markets and become less dependent on any one country.
Expanding access to E15 would create a more dependable domestic market for Illinois corn, support jobs across rural communities and give drivers another homegrown, cheaper fuel option.
text:
Illinois farmers did not start President Trump’s trade wars. But they are paying the price.

Fertilizer, fuel and equipment are more expensive than they were just a couple of years ago. Longtime customers overseas are looking elsewhere. And the financial uncertainty facing corn and soybean farmers is reaching across our state and the country into our homes. When the administration makes farming more expensive and selling crops more difficult, the consequences fall on everyone.

Illinois farmers lead the nation in soybean production, supporting jobs and businesses across rural communities while feeding families and industries thousands of miles away. But even the best product needs stable markets and reliable customers.

President Trump’s tariffs and unpredictable trade policies have threatened the export markets Illinois farmers spent generations developing. We have never fully recovered all of the markets we lost during the first Trump administration. As American trade relationships become less certain, competitors such as Brazil and Argentina are working to capture those customers. Illinois cannot sit idly by while that happens.

When the Trump administration creates uncertainty, states must step up. We must provide some stability and fight for the farmers, workers and families who keep our economies moving.

In Illinois, we are doing exactly that. Earlier this month, we signed an agreement with the Republic of Indonesia to expand trade, strengthen cooperation and create new opportunities for Illinois farmers, particularly soybean producers.

Indonesia is already an important trading partner. In 2024, Illinois exported more than $715 million in goods to Indonesia, including hundreds of millions of dollars in agricultural products, ranking third nationally in exports to Indonesia.

Our agreement creates a framework to deepen that relationship and pursue additional opportunities for Illinois-grown soybeans. For farmers in McLean County and throughout Illinois, stronger connections with Indonesian buyers could mean more customers and more certainty at a time when both are badly needed. No single agreement can replace every market disrupted by Trump’s trade policy. But developing new customers helps farmers diversify their markets and become less dependent on any one country.

We know this approach can work because we have pursued it together before.

In 2019, Illinois secured an agreement with Taiwan to purchase more than $2.2 billion in corn and soybeans. In 2022, we built on that relationship with another $2.6 billion commitment from Taiwan, including roughly $2 billion in soybeans and $600 million in corn. Those agreements show that sustained engagement can deliver stronger relationships abroad and real economic opportunities for communities at home.

Cut through the clutter! We deliver the news you need to stay informed about farm, food and rural issues. Sign up for a FREE month of Agri-Pulse here.

But helping farmers weather this uncertainty takes more than opening new export markets. It also means strengthening domestic demand and addressing the costs that eat into their bottom lines.

That is why Illinois has advocated for expansion of renewable fuels like biodiesel, sustainable aviation fuel and permanent, year-round sales of E15. Expanding access to E15 would create a more dependable domestic market for Illinois corn, support jobs across rural communities and give drivers another homegrown, cheaper fuel option.

Farmers should not have to depend on temporary federal waivers or wait year after year to know whether they will have access to a stronger domestic market. Congress should provide the certainty they need by making year-round E15 permanent.

As global conflicts have made access to fertilizer supplies severely strained and prices soar, we are also working to strengthen the fertilizer supply chain. A $2 billion investment by Cronus Chemicals in a fertilizer production facility in Tuscola will add domestic production capacity closer to Illinois farms and jobs.

As Illinois’ governor and senator, we have worked together to connect farmers with international buyers, strengthen relationships with trading partners and make sure Illinois businesses and workers are positioned to compete. But this hard work extends far beyond either of us.

It’s the farmers who make the case for Illinois soybeans and corn, agricultural organizations that connect producers with customers, businesses that identify new markets, universities that build international partnerships, and workers whose skills make Illinois products competitive.

The stakes are bigger than any one trade agreement. They are about whether a farmer can afford next season’s fertilizer, whether a family can manage its grocery bill, and whether communities across Illinois can count on good-paying jobs and a stronger future.

We cannot control the actions of the Trump administration. But we can make sure Illinois steps up, works together and fights for the certainty our farmers and families deserve.

That is the Illinois way. And it is a fight we intend to win together.

J.B. Pritzker is the governor of Illinois. Tammy Duckworth represents Illinois in the U.S. Senate.

title: Why is jet fuel so vulnerable to price shocks? - Fuel Oil News
description:
Jet Fuel (often called Jet A1 and sometimes called AVTUR = Aviation Turbine Fuel) is a type of paraffin that comes from a refinery’s Crude Distillation Unit (CDU).
Certain refining processes can increase the yield of jet fuel, but these are technically difficult and expensive.
But this is not the first time that jet fuel has been acutely affected by price shocks.
There is no such thing as a jet fuel refinery; you can’t just stop producing one product e.g., (jet fuel) if you want to carry on producing another (e.g., diesel).
At the same time, increasing jet fuel production at the expense of other grades is difficult and requires more complex refining technology.
text:
Over the last few months, there have been many column inches devoted to the shortage of jet fuel and consequent high prices, as a result of so much refining capacity being stuck “inside” the Strait of Hormuz.

Seeing as many of you will be jetting off on holiday at this time of the year, this month’s report will revisit what jet fuel is, why it is so prone to price shocks and what (if any) are the plans to find alternatives in a decarbonising world?

Jet Fuel (often called Jet A1 and sometimes called AVTUR = Aviation Turbine Fuel) is a type of paraffin that comes from a refinery’s Crude Distillation Unit (CDU). Gasoline (petrol) “sits” above Kerosene in the CDU, meaning the former boils first (at a lower temperature), giving it a more volatile and explosive nature.

Diesel lies lower than Kerosene in the CDU, which means it takes longer (higher temperature) to reach its boiling point, resulting in diesel being more stable than kero, but less flammable. Put all of this together and you have the reason that Kerosene is used to power aeroplanes.

Gasoline would not only be excessively hazardous, but its combustibility (whilst good for take-off) would be inefficient once the plane was airborne. Fuel consumption would be too rapid, and the plane would have to quickly land to refuel. Diesel on the other hand is much more fuel economic and releases energy in a more “conservative” fashion.

This means that it would be suitable for jet propulsion once the plane is airborne, but to take-off would require a runway that was about 5,000m long! Kerosene then is the perfect “in-between” grade; more stable and fuel efficient than petrol, but more combustible than diesel.

Refinery yields vary according to the crude slate (i.e., the type of crude that a CDU processes), but in general the amount of jet fuel produced from 1 barrel of Brent Crude (=159 litres) is around 25 litres (i.e., a 15% yield). By comparison, Brent yields 65 litres (~ 40% yield) of petrol and 55 litres (~ 35% yield) of diesel.

Certain refining processes can increase the yield of jet fuel, but these are technically difficult and expensive. Which means that whilst still not a specialist grade, jet fuel is most definitely not a ubiquitous, “everyday” grade such as gasoline or diesel.

This “weak” supply position versus strong and very specific demand dynamics (planes have to use it and there are no alternatives) is one of the reasons that jet fuel is prone to rapid price shocks. In Europe, the situation is exacerbated by a lack of indigenous production and an over-reliance on imports (the UK for example, imports 60% of its jet fuel).

This price volatility has obviously been amply illustrated in 2026, where the price of jet went up to $234 per barrel ($1,842.50 / tonne) in the aftermath of the Israeli and US attacks on Iran.

But this is not the first time that jet fuel has been acutely affected by price shocks. During the Arab Spring in 2012, Jet A1 topped $150 / bbl, even though the associated loss of production from Libya only concerned crude oil.

In the aftermath of the Russian invasion of Ukraine (widely seen as a crude and diesel crisis), jet fuel still hit $188 / bbl ($1,475.25 / tonne), whilst crude at the same time was “only” trading at $119.

And that same level of extreme price movements can also occur when prices tank, with jet often falling the fastest and furthest. In the pandemic, the UK saw a 30% reduction in jet fuel demand in Q1 2020, and this resulted in a drop in the price of Jet A1 from $83 / bbl at the start of that year ($652 per tonne) to $14 / bbl ($111 / tonne) by the end of April!

For refinery schedulers and aviation fuel buyers alike, the exposure to this kind of volatility is the stuff of nightmares. There is no such thing as a jet fuel refinery; you can’t just stop producing one product e.g., (jet fuel) if you want to carry on producing another (e.g., diesel).

At the same time, increasing jet fuel production at the expense of other grades is difficult and requires more complex refining technology. Buyers of course can hedge their exposure, but protection can only last so long and at some point, the hedge has to be renewed at a higher price.

Equally, hedging your jet fuel around $85 a barrel, only to see the price plummet to $15 / bbl is a fairly calamitous exercise – particularly if your planes are grounded through lack of demand.

Such is the torturous tightrope of supplying and buying jet fuel. Over the last few months, some commentators have pointed to Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF) as a neat solution to some of these problems.

Not only does it reduce emissions, but with the supply chain sitting outside the machinations in the Middle East, could SAF support supply resilience and help strip-out price volatility?

We will have a look at this topic next month, but in the meantime, happy holidays!

Portland
