text:
Name of the Project

Phelan Green electro-sustainable aviation fuel project.

Location

Saldanha Bay, Western Cape, South Africa.

Project Owner/s

Phelan Green Group, through its clean-fuels subsidiary Phelan eFuels.

Project Description

The project entails the development of a commercial-scale electro-sustainable aviation fuel (eSAF) facility.

The first phase is expected to produce about 35 000 t/y of eSAF, while full development of all phases is planned to increase production to about 140 000 t/y for export to EU and UK markets.

The initial phase will use a 200 MW electrolyser, forming the first tranche of a planned 800 MW deployment.

The facility will use renewable electricity, water and captured CO2 to produce SAF.

Renewable hydrogen produced through electrolysis will be combined with CO2 using Johnson Matthey’s HyCOgen technology to form carbon monoxide, which will be combined with additional hydrogen to make synthesis gas. Johnson Matthey and bp’s FT CANS technology will convert the synthesis gas into synthetic crude oil, which will subsequently be upgraded using Honeywell UOP’s Fischer Tropsch Unicracking technology to produce eSAF that meets aviation fuel standards.

Potential Job Creation

The project is expected to support thousands of local jobs across its multiple phases.

Capital Expenditure

R47-billion for the wider Phelan Green Hydrogen Project, of which the eSAF facility forms a core part. A separate capital cost for the eSAF facility has not been stated.

Planned Start/End Date

Construction is expected to start in the fourth quarter of 2026.

Latest Developments

Phelan Green Hydrogen announced in June 2026 that it had signed licence and engineering agreements with Johnson Matthey Catalyst Technologies for the first phase of the

project.

Johnson Matthey will provide its HyCOgen and FT CANS technologies, completing the core process-technology configuration for the facility.

The project will be Johnson Matthey’s first deployment of HyCOgen and FT CANS in Africa. The planned first-phase output is expected to be equivalent to as much as 6% of the EU’s and UK’s mandated eSAF volumes for 2030.

Key Contracts, Suppliers and Consultants

Johnson Matthey Catalyst Technologies (licence and engineering agreements covering HyCOgen and FT CANS technology; Honeywell UOP – Fischer Tropsch (unicracking process technology); and Sungrow Hydrogen (200 MW electrolyser supply agreement for the first tranche of the planned 800 MW electrolyser deployment).

text:
MechSE teaching assistant professor Jiajun He is leading an interdisciplinary research team that has received a 2026-27 seed fund from the Institute for Sustainability, Energy, and Environment (iSEE) to develop a circular approach for transforming food waste into sustainable fuels and carbon capture materials. He’s award was one of just four selected by iSEE for this year’s program, with each receiving $30K to launch new collaborations and generate preliminary results for larger research initiatives ().

The project, “Circular Carbon Platform for Food Waste: Integrated Production of Sustainable Aviation Fuel and CO2 Capture Materials,” brings together He with Yuanhui Zhang, a professor of agricultural and biological engineering at Illinois. The collaboration combines Zhang’s expertise in hydrothermal biomass conversion and fuel production with He’s work in porous carbon materials, adsorption science, and sustainability analysis.

Food waste represents a major underutilized carbon resource. Rather than treating it solely as waste, the researchers aim to use different carbon fractions to create valuable products.

“Food waste contains a significant amount of carbon that we currently do not fully utilize,” He said. “Our goal is to develop an integrated approach that converts different carbon fractions into useful products rather than generating another low-value waste stream.”

Their proposed platform will first convert food waste through hydrothermal liquefaction (HTL), producing an energy-rich biocrude that can be upgraded into sustainable aviation fuel (SAF), along with carbon-rich solid residues.

He’s group will transform the solid residues into hierarchical porous carbon materials for CO2 capture through controlled activation and pyrolysis. By tailoring their pore structures and surface chemistry, the researchers aim to improve the materials’ CO2 adsorption performance.

The team will also investigate how food waste components, including lipids, proteins, and carbohydrates, transform during hydrothermal processing and how carbon is partitioned among fuels, solids, gases, and other products. Techno-economic analysis and life-cycle assessment will evaluate the economic feasibility and environmental benefits of the integrated process.

“The idea is to connect waste-to-fuel conversion with carbon capture materials in the same platform,” He said. “By integrating fuel production, carbon capture, and sustainability analysis, we hope to establish a new pathway for circular carbon utilization.”

The seed project will generate preliminary data to support larger external research initiatives in sustainable aviation fuel, carbon management, and the circular bioeconomy.

text:
Nova Pangaea Technologies has completed an endurance trial campaign at its demonstration facility in Teesside, United Kingdom, validating continuous production of bioethanol from woody residues for use in sustainable aviation fuel (SAF), the company said, according to energynews.pro.

The trials were conducted as part of the Speedbird programme, which is being carried out with British Airways and LanzaJet and supported by the UK government through the Advanced Fuels Fund.

Nova Pangaea’s REFNOVA process converts materials such as wood chips, sawdust and wheat straw into bioethanol. The ethanol produced through this process cannot be used directly as aviation fuel and must undergo further processing using LanzaJet’s Alcohol-to-Jet (ATJ) technology to produce certified SAF.

The process also produces biochar as a by-product. Nova Pangaea said the biochar stores carbon and allows the overall process to be described as carbon negative.

The trial campaign was designed to demonstrate that the process could operate continuously and reliably for periods representative of commercial operations. Nova Pangaea said this validation was an important step in giving investors confidence before a decision is taken on building the company’s first commercial plant.

The wider Speedbird programme aims to establish several bioethanol production plants in the UK to support a domestic SAF supply chain.

The company is currently led by chief executive Stewart Stewart, who took up the position on January 13, 2026. He succeeded Sarah Ellerby, who had led the company at least until November 2022. Gerald Koch is chairman of the board.

The technology is also intended to provide an alternative source of raw materials for SAF production. The industry currently relies heavily on used cooking oil, but this resource is considered insufficient to meet the aviation sector’s growing demand for SAF.

Nova Pangaea’s approach uses residual plant-based material and is designed to process different types of woody and agricultural residues. The company did not specify the exact material used during the latest trial campaign.

The successful continuous production trials at Teesside mark a technical milestone for the Speedbird programme. However, Nova Pangaea has not provided a timeline for moving to commercial-scale production, with the next major step expected to depend on an investment decision for the first industrial-scale plant.

description:

text:
Marks Fifth Consecutive Year at London Climate Action Week, Reinforcing Its Leadership in Asia's Climate Finance

Our responsibility is no longer just to reduce our footprint, but to expand our handprint- mobilizing capital to build a resilient, net zero Asia.”

— Cathay FHC President, Chang-Ken Lee

LONDON, UNITED KINGDOM, August 27, 2026 /EINPresswire.com/ -- As climate change, energy security and geopolitical uncertainty reshape the global economy, Asia is emerging as one of the world's most important regions for climate investment and energy transition. At London Climate Action Week 2026, Cathay Financial Holdings (Cathay FHC) announced that it has joined the 24/7 Carbon-Free Energy Coalition, becoming the world's first and only financial institution to participate in this trailblazing initiative. The milestone reflects Cathay FHC's long-standing commitment to advancing energy transition through sustainable finance across Asia.

The announcement was made during Cathay FHC's fifth consecutive participation in Europe's largest climate week, where President Chang-Ken Lee joined international leaders from governments, businesses and financial institutions to discuss how cross-sector collaboration can drive climate action in an increasingly fragmented world.

The milestone underscores Cathay FHC's growing stature as one of Asia's leading sustainable finance institutions, leveraging capital, strategic partnerships and innovation to accelerate the region's transition toward a resilient, low-carbon economy.

Raising the Bar for Corporate Climate Leadership

Cathay FHC has consistently been at the forefront of sustainable finance and corporate decarbonization in Asia. In 2022, it became the first financial institution in Taiwan to join the RE100 initiative, committing to source 100% renewable electricity across its operations. By 2025, renewable electricity accounted for more than 50% of Cathay FHC's total electricity consumption.

Beyond its own operations, Cathay FHC has become Taiwan's largest green commercial property owner, enabling tenants to share renewable electricity through innovative energy management. Over the past year, Cathay FHC facilitated the delivery of more than 54 million kWh of renewable electricity to over 70 corporate tenants, helping businesses accelerate their renewable energy transition and collectively reduce carbon emissions.

Joining the 24/7 Carbon-Free Energy Coalition represents the next stage of Cathay FHC's climate strategy. Unlike conventional annual renewable energy targets, the initiative encourages organizations to match every hour of electricity consumption with carbon-free energy generated on the same power grid—widely recognized as the next frontier in corporate clean electricity procurement.

Mobilizing Sustainable Finance Across Asia

"Climate change and geopolitical uncertainty have fundamentally changed the operating environment for businesses and financial institutions," said Chang-Ken Lee, President of Cathay Financial Holdings.

"Building resilience is no longer optional. As a financial institution, our responsibility extends beyond reducing our own environmental footprint. We must also expand our positive handprint by mobilizing capital toward the industries, technologies and communities that will power Asia's net-zero transition."

Cathay FHC continues to expand its sustainable finance portfolio across the region through investments and financing for geothermal energy in Indonesia, onshore wind power in Vietnam, and sustainable aviation fuel projects in Singapore. Together with strategic international partnerships, these initiatives strengthen Cathay FHC's long-term resilience while accelerating climate solutions across Asia.

Building Bankable Climate Solutions

Recognizing that many climate solutions require new financing models, Cathay FHC is integrating the strengths of its banking, insurance, investment and asset management businesses to improve the investability and bankability of sustainable projects.

One recent example is Cathay United Bank's participation in the Green Investments Partnership (GIP) managed by Pentagreen Capital, making it the first Taiwanese bank to join the blended finance platform supporting sustainable infrastructure development across Southeast Asia.

Beyond providing capital, Cathay FHC is evolving into a long-term transition partner, working alongside clients to strengthen resilience and accelerate their net-zero transformation.

Cathay FHC also believes that a successful energy transition must be inclusive. Through its longstanding partnership with the Asian Venture Philanthropy Network (AVPN) and participation in the Asia's Clean Energy Transition Initiative (ASCENT), together with organizations including the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) and the Asian Development Bank (ADB), Cathay FHC supports the People-Centric Energy Transition Catalytic Fund, promoting a transition that benefits both people and the planet.

Connecting Global Capital with Asia's Climate Future

title: Every Tuesday Morning, Iowa's Mitchell Hora Explains Washington To The Corn Belt
description:
At 7:45 on a Tuesday morning at the end of June, Mitchell Hora sat in front of a camera and started taking questions.

text:
At 7:45 on a Tuesday morning at the end of June, Mitchell Hora sat in front of a camera and started taking questions. A farmer named Russ wanted to know why the new scoring system was so sensitive to region. Lanny wanted to know what it meant for the ethanol plant in Columbus, Nebraska. Then, a farmer named Tim came off mute and asked the question sitting underneath all the others. When, exactly, is any of this going to be final?

It was the 101st episode of CI Chit Chat, a call-in show Hora hosts every Tuesday from 7:45 a.m. to 8:15 a.m. “It took us 100 episodes to get 45Z rule to happen,” he told the group. “But we did it.”

Video Courtesy Continuum Ag

The rule he was referring to sets the terms under which a farmer’s growing practices can be counted and paid for under a federal biofuel tax credit. Four days earlier, the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) had finally published it, and Hora, who said he had read all 101 pages, had spent most of the previous four years walking farmers through a program that did not yet work.

Hora farms in Ainsworth, in Washington County, Iowa, alongside his father, Brian. In 2020, the National Association of Conservation Districts recognized them as Soil Health Champions, noting that Brian is the sixth generation on the operation and Mitchell is the seventh. Mitchell is also the founder and chief executive of Continuum Ag, which he started in the fall of 2015, during his junior year at Iowa State University. The family farm supplied the proof of concept. Hora has said that his family began experimenting with no-till in 1978 and added cover crops in 2013, and that the operation has cut synthetic fertilizer use by 45% and pesticide use by 75% while holding yields steady. “So, we understand how to allow farmers to be successful and change their practices by utilizing data because we’ve done it ourselves and have helped many other farmers do the same. The key thing is that farmers have to drive sustainability,” he told Cisco. “I started Continuum Ag as a consulting company to help my family farm and help other local family farms understand soil health and access better data tools to manage their farms.” The goal has grown to “helping 1 million farmers improve their profitability through improved soil health.”

Photo Courtesy Continuum Ag

The company began as a consultancy built around the Haney Soil Health Test, a lab method for measuring biological activity in soil rather than only its chemistry. That work eventually became a software platform called TopSoil, as the soil health data intelligence company helps farmers map their fields, gain valuable insights, and evaluate new farming practices to achieve economic resilience and sustainability.

A carbon intensity score, or CI score, measures the carbon footprint of producing agricultural products, like a single bushel of grain. A score of 0.0 means the bushel is net carbon neutral. The standard score for corn now sits at 27.4 grams of carbon dioxide equivalent per megajoule of energy, according to the company, adding that “the lower the CI Score, the more attractive that production is for end users.” In fact, gaining CI Certification enables farmers to demand a price premium from the biofuel producers, who in turn receive special tax credits for low-carbon fuels.

The practices that move a score are ones many farmers already use. Lancaster Farming reported in April 2024 that Continuum Ag had scored 185 million bushels of corn and found an average score of 10.7, far below the roughly 29-point default in use at the time, with the strongest operations landing in the negative teens and twenties. More cover crops and manure, less tillage and reduced fuel and synthetic fertilizer inputs, better nitrogen efficiency, and higher yields all pull the number down.

Hora explained during his June press conference that an ethanol plant’s score gets rounded to the nearest multiple of five, so the value arrives in steps. Every five points a plant knocks off its score is worth up to about 10 cents a gallon, which he put at roughly 29 cents a bushel, before any of it is shared with the farmer who grew the corn. “But the point of all this is we now know that the practices can generate enough CI reduction to make this a carrot worth going after,” he said.

Photo Courtesy Continuum Ag

For most of the company’s life, none of that measurement paid. Congress created the Section 45Z Clean Fuel Production Credit in 2022, and the credit rewards biofuel producers for lowering their fuel’s carbon footprint. Grain accounts for roughly half of a gallon of biofuel’s carbon footprint, according to Continuum Ag. But the federal government never issued the rules explaining how on-farm practices would be counted.

Hora built the verification systems, audit relationships, and software anyway, then waited. “I’ve been right on the bet,” he told Barn Talk in an interview. “I’ve just been wrong on the timing.”

An audience carried the company through the gap. In November 2023, the company launched the Billion Bushel Challenge, an effort to get a billion bushels of corn scored in a single year and to raise awareness that farmers can make money by growing low-carbon corn. An annual gathering called the TopSoil Summit drew 250 people from more than 15 states and three countries in 2023. A single webinar on sustainable aviation fuel guidance in May 2024 pulled more than 400 farmers and still ran out of time before it ran out of questions. In conversation with Barn Talk, he called sustainable aviation fuel a “100 billion gallon a year opportunity,” up from the current 17 billion gallons.

On June 25, 2026, USDA announced a final rule establishing how the carbon intensity of biofuel feedstock crops gets quantified, reported, and verified. It covers field corn, soybeans, sorghum, and spring canola. The rule was published in the Federal Register on June 29 and took effect July 29, 2026.

Hora did not get everything he asked for. He had lobbied for a tracking system called book-and-claim, which would let a farmer sell the grain to one buyer and the carbon data to another. During the press conference, he reported that of roughly 114 public comments, 60 addressed traceability, and about 75% of those favored book-and-claim. USDA instead kept mass balance, which requires the grain and its data to travel together into the biofuel supply chain.

His plainest explanation of what that means arrived on a later broadcast. Picture two grain bins, he said, except digital: one holds low-carbon bushels, one holds conventional bushels, and a farmer needs verified data to get into the first one. “There ain’t much low-carbon corn out there right now, because we haven’t verified all of it,” he explained, so “that digital grain bin over here is empty. And that’s where Continuum fits in to help farmers get their data organized, get it scored, get it verified, so that your corn or soybeans goes in the low carbon bin, not the conventional bin.” On his own farm, the arrangement means trucking corn to an ethanol plant rather than selling it to the neighbor who feeds hogs to tap into 45Z.

One step remains. The Internal Revenue Service (IRS) issued proposed regulations for the credit on February 3, 2026, and has not yet finalized them. Hora noted in a later episode that the agency has signaled a November target, while adding that he has learned to hold his optimism loosely. The credit expires at the end of 2029, Hora told Tim, which means the window narrows every month: “We need to capitalize on this thing, make hay while the sun is shining.” He told Barn Talk, “I do think that there’s going to be some money moving by the end of the year. Farmers getting paid by the end of the year.”

Photo Courtesy Continuum Ag

Because the data now has to follow the grain, the work has shifted from farmers to the people who buy from them. Within weeks of the rule taking effect, Hora said he had spoken with more than 100 of the country’s 192 ethanol plants. Counting soybean crushers, he put the universe of biofuel producers at about 250, alongside some 5,000 grain elevators.

Many of those relationships predate the rule. Siouxland Energy Cooperative in Sioux Center, Iowa, agreed in March 2024 to buy low-carbon bushels certified by Continuum. Aztalan Bio, an ethanol producer in Johnson Creek, Wisconsin, announced a similar arrangement in June 2026. Geography favors the effort. Lancaster Farming counted 41 ethanol plants in Iowa alone, against two in the entire Mid-Atlantic.

For a farmer trying to figure out whether any of this applies, Hora lays out three steps. Calculate the score first. Then find out where last year’s crop actually went, and whether that buyer intends to run a program. “And if they’re not, we’re happy to have those conversations with them.”

Photo Courtesy Continuum Ag

The recognition has come from several directions. The Iowa Department of Agriculture gave Hora its Environmental Excellence Award in 2023, and his work was entered into the Congressional Record in June 2025. He was named to the Forbes 30 Under 30 list announced in December 2021. In June 2025, Sen. Joni Ernst named Continuum Ag her Small Business of the Week, noting, “Since 2015, Continuum Ag has rooted themselves in helping farmers manage and improve their soil health. Partnering with over 40 states and 20 countries, Continuum Ag continues to encourage regenerative agricultural practices that enable farmers to make data-driven decisions.”

Marking the company’s tenth year, Hora closed a short film with a line that read less like a victory lap than a starting gun. “We feel like we’re just getting started.” And they’re doing it all while remaining “very passionate about adding jobs to the local area, keeping those small towns alive,” which is part and parcel of the agricultural story, he told Barn Talk.

Hora was recently interviewed at the Iowa State Fair by Barn Talk, one of the country’s most-listened-to agriculture podcasts, with 274 million views to date. Stay tuned for the Barn Talk episode.

Investing.com - S&P Global Ratings upgraded its issuer credit rating on Calumet Inc. to ’B-’ from ’CCC+’ today, citing stronger-than-expected earnings in the first half of 2026 and improving credit metrics. The rating agency also raised its issue-level ratings one notch to ’B+’ for the senior secured debt and ’B-’ for the unsecured debt. The outlook is stable.

Calumet’s earnings and cash flow grew in the first half of 2026 on the back of high margins for specialty oils, wide fuel crack spreads, and high renewable fuel margins. Performance was particularly strong in the second quarter despite two planned turnarounds and several weeks of planned downtime at its renewable fuels facility, Montana Renewables LLC. S&P Global Ratings expects weighted-average adjusted debt to EBITDA of 6x-7x, with the metric being stronger than this over the next 12 months.

In July 2026, the company redeemed its existing $100 million 9.75% senior unsecured notes due 2028 using liquidity from a tack-on issuance to its senior notes due 2031 earlier in the year. Calumet’s nearest material debt maturity is its $325 million senior unsecured notes due July 2028. S&P Global Ratings forecasts free operating cash flow will remain strong in 2027 due to earnings momentum and the continued sale of the 45Z production tax credits in the secondary market.

The company is progressing on MaxSAF, its project to expand sustainable aviation fuel production at Montana Renewables. During the second quarter of 2026, SAF capacity increased to about 60 million gallons per year. Management plans to repurpose an existing reactor at Calumet’s specialty asphalt site this winter, which will bring capacity to 120-150 million gallons by spring of 2027. By the end of 2028, management aims to increase total throughput and raise SAF capacity to about 200 million gallons per year.

As of June 30, 2026, the surge in RIN prices increased reported obligations to about $480 million from $169 million at the end of 2025. S&P Global Ratings does not add these obligations to its adjusted debt balances but could change this if the likelihood of payments by the company increases. The rating agency’s key assumption at the current rating is that Calumet will not have to pay against its RINs obligations in the next 12 months.

Spearheading the shift to low-emission aviation

Sustainability is central to Shell & MOH’s business strategy. We facilitate green aviation practices by scaling the distribution of Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF) across Greek and Bulgarian airports, extending SAF availability to all airline segments — while actively reducing our technical joint ventures’ own operational emissions to lead by example.

Promoting the adoption of SAF

SAF is a biofuel that reduces lifecycle carbon emissions by a minimum of 80% compared to conventional jet fuel, making it one of the most impactful ways to decarbonise air travel. Shell & MOH Aviation is leading the way in making SAF readily available at Greek airports — offered locally, not through global mass-balance systems — guaranteeing that SAF is physically used in Greek and Bulgarian aviation operations and delivers direct CO₂ reductions.

Supporting infrastructure and market development

We collaborate with stakeholders such as aviation authorities and airports to ensure sufficient infrastructure for SAF storage and distribution, and we supply SAF even at the non-Union airports of Kalamata and Araxos, driving sustainability market development.

Committed to reducing our own CO₂ emissions

As part of our sustainability strategy, we are not only helping the aviation industry reduce emissions but also taking significant steps to reduce our own footprint — including reducing Scope 1 and 2 emissions.

text:
KROHNE is highlighting its portfolio of process instrumentation designed for sustainable aviation fuel production, with measurement technologies aimed at improving reliability and efficiency as SAF facilities scale up production.

SAF production combines conventional refining processes with renewable feedstocks such as used cooking oil, edible oils, ethanol and biogas. According to KROHNE, the combination creates measurement challenges throughout feedstock pretreatment, hydrotreatment and isomerization, hydrogen management and custody transfer.

“The SAF industry brings together two very different worlds,” said Yannick Farine, industry manager for biofuels and bioenergy at KROHNE. “Success depends on understanding the behavior of renewable feedstocks upstream while also meeting the demands of downstream refining. Our goal is to help customers optimize processes, reduce maintenance and build SAF plants they can rely on for years to come.”

KROHNE offers instrumentation for flow and level measurement as well as specialized equipment for more demanding SAF applications. The company is applying its experience in edible oils, ethanol, biogas and oil and gas to help producers select instrumentation for different stages of SAF production.

Among the technologies being deployed are ultrasonic flowmeters, which have no internal restrictions, capillaries or moving parts. KROHNE said the equipment can be used with abrasive feedstocks, hydrogen-rich streams, high-pressure steam and other challenging applications. Certain ultrasonic meters can operate at temperatures up to 600 C and at high pressures for both liquids and gases.

The company also offers straight-tube Coriolis mass flowmeters for applications requiring high accuracy and direct mass measurement. The full-bore design is intended to reduce wear when handling abrasive feedstocks, while entrained gas management technology supports measurement under two-phase flow conditions at temperatures up to 400 C.

KROHNE said the instrumentation can help SAF producers manage feedstock variability, hydrogen utilization and maintenance requirements while supporting mass-balance and yield monitoring.

In addition to individual instruments, KROHNE supplies integrated systems for SAF facilities, including custody transfer metering skids, leak detection systems and blending skids.

text:
LINCOLN, Neb. (DTN) -- With the Trump administration just days away from announcing a decision that could grant nearly two billion gallons in small-refinery exemptions to the Renewable Fuel Standard, agriculture and biofuels groups warned President Donald Trump on Thursday that doing so would damage agriculture and the rural economy.

With the possibility the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency could grant around 1.8 billion gallons worth of exemptions, biofuels and farmer interest groups who are part of a rural voting block that helped elect Trump twice told the president in a letter to "stand strong against" attempts to undermine the RFS.

"History is unambiguous: The last time the Environmental Protection Agency granted SREs at the scale being contemplated, the biofuel industry lost $6.4 billion, renewable fuel credits collapsed by up to 78% and gas prices rose 12%," the groups told Trump.

"RIN prices clearly don't drive gas prices. The only winners were refiners in a sector that today is reporting record profitability, even as American farmers face down another year of negative incomes."

The letter is signed by Clean Fuels Alliance America, Growth Energy, National Corn Growers Association, National Oilseed Processors Association, Renewable Fuels Association, Bunge, Darling Ingredients, Green Plains, International Flavors & Fragrances Inc. (IFF), Novonesis, Poet LLC, National Farmers Union and the American Soybean Association.

DESTROY BIOFUEL DEMAND

They told Trump reducing blending volumes in the RFS program with SREs will "destroy the biofuel demand that is now working to restore the rural economy" and reduce fuel costs for drivers.

"Your administration's actions to date to restore certainty to the Renewable Fuel Standard have provided a strong signal that the United States is committed to expanding domestic fuel production, supporting farm income, and reducing reliance on foreign energy sources," the letter said. The 2026 and 2027 RFS volumes finalized in March 2026, the groups said, represented a "decisive, market-defining commitment" to American biofuels, domestic agriculture and the rural economy.

"Since finalization of the Set 2 RVO, more than a dozen companies have increased production or announced investments in crush capacity, renewable diesel and sustainable aviation fuel infrastructure, with executives and company statements directly citing RFS policy as the driver," the letter said.

AGRICULTURE INVESTMENTS

They said the U.S. soybean processing industry has invested over $7 billion to expand crushing capacity by more than 25%, which is enough to process two-thirds of the soybeans grown in the U.S.

The groups pointed to EPA estimates that the 2026 RVO will create $31 billion in value for American corn and soybean oil. USDA estimates a $3 billion to $4 billion increase in net farm income directly attributable to the Set 2 RVO, supporting more than 100,000 new agricultural and manufacturing jobs.

"Today, these gains are at risk from pending SREs," the letter said.

"As your administration considers pending SRE decisions for the 2025 compliance year, we urge you to keep any SREs granted consistent with the projected level of exempted volumes that were used by EPA to establish the current program structure in the final Set 2 RVO, with the reallocation of any waived gallons in 2026 and 2027."

The groups said exemptions were intended by Congress to provide "targeted relief in cases of genuine disproportionate economic hardship" because of the RFS -- "not to provide a pathway for a select group of refiners to secure regulatory arbitrage."

EPA has been consistent in saying the price of RINs, or renewable identification numbers, do not increase gas prices, the letter said.

"The EPA's Set 2 RVO presented a reasonable approach to restoring much of the renewable fuel volume lost to SREs granted in recent years," the groups said.

"But if EPA grants an amount of SREs well above the amount projected in the Set 2 RVO, it will decimate the demand signal that the Set 2 rule was designed to create. The consequences would be severe and immediate: biofuel markets would collapse as excess SREs reduce blending requirements. This would remove demand for corn, soybean oil, canola and other feedstocks, translating directly to lower farm prices and weaker rural economies."

The letter said consumers would lose "lower-cost fuel options" as "excess SREs would tighten the fuel market and undermine" the administration's stated goal of lowering energy costs.

"Investment in renewable fuel infrastructure would stall, signaling to every future investor that U.S. biofuel commitments cannot be trusted," the letter said.

text:
On behalf of America’s farmers, biofuel producers, oilseed processors, feedstock suppliers, and rural communities,

we write to thank you for your Administration’s commitment to American energy dominance, domestic

manufacturing, reducing consumer prices at the pump, and strengthening rural America. We also urge you to stand

strong against misguided efforts to increase the use of small refinery exemptions (SREs). Reducing blending volumes

in the RFS program through the use of SREs will destroy the biofuel demand that is now working to restore the rural

economy and reduce fuel costs for drivers.

History is unambiguous: the last time the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) granted SREs at the scale

being contemplated, the biofuel industry lost $6.4 billion, renewable fuel credits collapsed by up to 78 percent,

and gas prices rose 12 percent – RIN prices clearly don’t drive gas prices. The only winners were refiners in a

sector that today is reporting record profitability, even as American farmers face down another year of negative

incomes.

Your Administration’s actions to date to restore certainty to the Renewable Fuel Standard (RFS) have provided a

strong signal that the United States is committed to expanding domestic fuel production, supporting farm income,

and reducing reliance on foreign energy sources. The Set 2 Renewable Volume Obligation (RVO) for 2026 and 2027,

finalized in March of 2026, represented a decisive, market-defining commitment to American biofuels, domestic

agriculture, and rural economic growth.

Since finalization of the Set 2 RVO, more than a dozen companies have increased production or announced

investments in crush capacity, renewable diesel, and sustainable aviation fuel infrastructure, with executives and

company statements directly citing RFS policy as the driver. The U.S. soybean processing industry has invested over

$7 billion to expand crushing capacity by over 25% – enough to process 2/3 of the soybeans grown in the U.S.,

reducing reliance on the Chinese market. EPA estimates that the 2026 RVO will create $31 billion in value for

American corn and soybean oil and USDA estimates a $3 to $4 billion increase in net farm income directly

attributable to the Set 2 RVO finalization, supporting more than 100,000 new agricultural and manufacturing jobs.

Today, these gains are at risk from pending SREs.

As your Administration considers pending SRE decisions for the 2025 compliance year, we urge you to keep any SREs

granted consistent with the projected level of exempted volumes that were used by EPA to establish the current

program structure in the final Set 2 RVO, with the reallocation of any waived gallons in 2026 and 2027.

SREs were intended by Congress to provide targeted relief in cases of genuine disproportionate economic hardship

as a result of the RFS – not to provide a pathway for a select group of refiners to secure regulatory arbitrage. EPA has

consistently determined over the last decades that RIN prices do not increase gas prices, and evidence from specific

periods of high RIN prices shows no corresponding increase in gas prices attributable to RINs.

The EPA’s Set 2 RVO presented a reasonable approach to restoring much of the renewable fuel volume lost to SREs

granted in recent years. But if EPA grants an amount of SREs well above the amount projected in the Set 2 RVO, it will

decimate the demand signal that the Set 2 rule was designed to create.

The consequences would be severe and immediate: biofuel markets would collapse as excess SREs reduce blending

requirements. This would remove demand for corn, soybean oil, canola, and other feedstocks, translating directly to

lower farm prices and weaker rural economies. Consumers would lose lower-cost fuel options as excess SREs would

tighten the fuel market and undermine the Administration’s stated goal of lowering energy costs. Investment in

renewable fuel infrastructure would stall, signaling to every future investor that U.S. biofuel commitments cannot be

trusted. Reallocation of waived gallons above the levels published in the Set 2 RVO at some uncertain time in the

future beyond 2027 won’t mitigate what will be irreparable harm today.

We respectfully urge your Administration to implement the final rule consistent with EPA’s own assumptions and

reject proposals to increase SRE waivers beyond the levels in the final Set 2 RVO, protect the farmers and rural

communities who depend on strong RFS volumes to drive commodity markets, take action to lower prices at the

pump, and preserve domestic energy security with American biofuel production.

text:
(For the full report view the PDF available in the blue panel)

Foreword

Aviation continues to bring significant benefits to society, but it must do so while addressing its environmental and public health responsibilities.

Ultrafine particles (UFPs) are an area where scientific understanding is developing quickly, and where the sector has an important role to play in generating evidence and responding to what that evidence shows.

This White Paper sets out a view of what we know – and do not yet know – about UFPs in the aviation context. Its focus is understandably on emissions from aircraft engines, given the emerging scientific interest in combustion related UFPs, but it is also important to note that brake and tyre wear are additional sources of particulate emissions and merit further consideration as the evidence base develops.

The paper highlights the progress already made in improving air quality, the potential for further reductions through measures such as Sustainable Aviation Fuel, and the research now needed to understand exposure pathways and health implications more fully.

The Board welcomes Sustainable Aviation’s commitment to strengthening capability in UFP measurement and analysis, including its long-term investment in research. We strongly support this and look forward to Sustainable Aviation doing even more in the coming years to help the sector better understand and reduce UFP emissions.

Sustainable Aviation Advisory Board

The Sustainable Aviation Advisory Board works with Sustainable Aviation’s Council to provide independent advice and feedback.

Executive Summary

Sustainable Aviation (SA) is a coalition of UK airlines, airports, aerospace manufacturers, fuel producers and partners all committed to delivering net zero carbon aviation by 2050, and to minimising the aviation sector’s noise and air quality impacts.

For more than 20 years, Sustainable Aviation members have worked together to build a more sustainable future for our industry and ensure that aviation can continue to deliver substantial benefits to the UK and its economy.

Improving air quality around airports is a priority for SA and wider industry. We recognise that Ultrafine Particles (UFPs), defined as particulate matter with diameters less than 100 nanometers (PM0.1), have emerged as a pollutant of growing scientific interest, and that UFPs present unique challenges due to their small size, high number concentrations, and potential health impacts.

SA and its members remain committed to understanding and reducing these emissions through collaborative research, technological innovation, and policy engagement.

We first published a report on UK aviation and air quality in 2017. This concluded that aircraft emissions contribute 1% of the UK nitrogen oxide (NOx) emissions and 0.1% of UK particulate (PM10) emissions.

This White Paper provides the aviation industry’s current view on ambient local air quality, an overview of the recent research on UFPs, challenges facing the industry, and opportunities to further understand mitigation options for UFPs moving forward.

This paper sets out Sustainable Aviation’s position on UFPs. It reviews:

Current understanding of ambient air quality and UFPs in the aviation context.

Emerging research, including studies at Los Angeles International Airport and Boston Logan International Airport, which have found elevated concentrations of UFPs correlated with aviation.

Mitigation opportunities, such as the deployment of Sustainable Aviation Fuels (SAF), hydrogen and electric aircraft and decarbonising airfield operations. SAFs have shown promise in reducing UFP emissions and improving air quality outcomes.

Research gaps, particularly in UFP measurement standardisation in the aviation context. SA is actively supporting research to close these gaps, including funding a PhD programme focused on UFP measurement at airports.

2. Air Quality

This section provides an overview of Sustainable Aviation’s previous publication on air quality and an update on our view of the current ambient air quality environment around airports.

2.1 Local Air Quality 2017 – 2025

The 2017 UK Aviation and Air Quality report explored the effect of UK aviation on local air quality and outlined the range of activities that were being undertaken throughout the industry to minimise emissions. This paper also considered emerging opportunities to further improve local air quality around airports/from aviation.

The findings in this paper describe the following elements that are still relevant to today’s operations:

Air emissions sources at and near to airports;

Air quality near to airports; monitoring, information sharing, air quality action plans;

Initiatives to reduce air quality emissions; and

Opportunities for improvement through collaboration.

In the eight years since the 2017 paper was published, concentrations of NO2, PM10 and PM2.5 in urban areas, including around UK airports, have been improving and are generally compliant with air quality standards.

More stringent air quality objectives for PM2.5 came into force in 2023 (DEFRA, 2023). These outline the air quality target values, long-term objectives and legally binding limit values for concentrations of major air pollutants that impact public health and ecosystems in the UK.

case study

Since 2017, air quality monitoring at Heathrow Airport shows a sustained improving trend in regulated pollutants, including nitrogen dioxide (NO2), PM10, and PM2.5. Current concentrations are below legally mandated limit values, reflecting the success of mitigation efforts such as cleaner ground operations, improved traffic management, and fleet modernisation.

This trend is mirrored at other major UK airports, where similar reductions in regulated emissions have been observed. These improvements are consistent with national air quality objectives and demonstrate the aviation sector’s commitment to reducing its environmental footprint.

As fleets continue to modernise with newer, cleaner aircraft and with increased uptake of SAF there is a strong likelihood that UFP emissions have already declined. However, due to the absence of consistent monitoring, these reductions have not been quantified. Such mitigation measures are discussed further in Section 4.

SA considers the existing 2017 paper a relevant reflection of the industry’s current local air quality position, as it relates to regulated air quality emissions.

The 2017 paper identifies UFP as an emerging scientific interest:

In addition to the pollutants discussed in the above, for which there is a strong and established evidence base, a smaller type of PM – ultra-fine particles (UFP) – are an emerging scientific interest. These particles are a sub-setof the emissions above.

Scientific research into UFP is still in its infancy, however Airports Council International has published a report (Airports Council International Europe, 2013) which provides an overview of available information on UFP and current understanding in an aviation context. This report was supported by airports that are members of Airport Council International. The report concludes that current understanding of average, long-term concentrations of UFP at airports, particularly in terms of dose effect is insufficient to establish any relationships. A review of studies of UFP concentrations shows that concentrations of UFP at airports are not notably higher than results from non-airport locations. Airports will continue to support further research in this area.

UK Aviation and Air Quality Report Sustainable Aviation, 2017 (page 49).

2.2 A focus on addressing UFPs

Since our Local Air Quality report was published, UFPs have become an area of intense interest with significant amounts of active research ongoing.

This paper addresses and reflects updated UFP research as our understanding of the relationship between UFPs and aviation develops.

To better understand the impacts of UFPs on air quality and the impacts of aviation on concentration patterns, we are engaging in and supporting targeted research in this field.

More detail on this can be found in Section 4.5.

3. Ultrafine Particles

This section provides an overview of Sustainable Aviation’s current understanding of the sources of ambient UFPs, their impacts on human health, regulatory limits and emerging research.

3.1 Sources of UFPs

UFPs are primarily emitted through combustion processes. According to the UK Government’s Air Quality Expert Group (Air Quality Expert Group, 2018), road vehicles are the major source of UFP emissions in the UK. However, there is growing scientific understanding that shows that exhaust emissions from aircraft engines include a relatively high concentration of UFPs. How these affect population areas, relative to other sources, is currently less well understood.

Studies, including those at Los Angeles International Airport (Dane Westerdahl, 2008) , Boston Logan International Airport (Chung et al., 2023) , and Barcelona-El Prat Airport (S. Ridolfo, 2024) , have found that elevated concentrations of UFPs are correlated with aircraft flight paths at longer-range distances from airport boundaries (about 10–15 km) compared to other aircraft emissions like NOx or PM, which are not

detectable at those distances. The Barcelona study also revealed significantly higher UFP concentrations within the airport, with aircraft operations, particularly taxiing and take-off, being major contributors. Historically, most concerns about UFPs at airports have been centred around occupational exposure, i.e. for those working on the airfield.

In 2014, Copenhagen Airport was required to set up a permanent UFP monitoring programme and “environmental” operating procedures to reduce aircraft emissions and UFP exposure (Stacey, 2019).

In March 2024, a court ruling mandated that the Dutch government must provide better protection for residents around Schiphol against UFPs and noise pollution (Schiphol, 2025).

Section 4 explores opportunities to reduce these emissions. However, as road vehicle emissions improve and shift to EVs, the proportion of UFP emissions from aviation will become greater.

As aviation’s relative contribution to UFP emissions grows, it is important to recognise the significant progress already made in reducing UFPs from other sources, particularly road transport. The removal of sulphur from petrol and diesel fuels has led to measurable improvements in urban air quality. Notably, research by the University of Birmingham (A.M. Jones, 2012) has shown a marked reduction in UFP concentrations at London Marylebone following these fuel specification changes. The study inferred that during the latter part of 2007 a 65% reduction occurred in the emissions of fine particles relative to NOx, from vehicles at Marylebone Road.

3.2 Impacts of UFPs on human health

We note that there is no consensus on health implications of UFPs (Stacey, 2019); however, a growing body of research suggests there may be health impacts. Like PM10 and PM2.5, UFPs have been associated with cardiovascular and respiratory health impacts. Due to their much smaller size, UFPs can penetrate more deeply into the lungs where they have been shown to enter the blood stream and end up in vital body organs, including the brain.

The World Health Organisation (WHO) global air quality guidelines (WHO, 2021) recognised that there is growing evidence of toxicology effects of UFPs, however, concluded that the evidence is not sufficient to formulate air quality guideline levels for exposure. The EU is also looking into new monitoring techniques.

The aviation industry is committed to the collection and monitoring of data that can be utilised by healthcare professionals for their assessment. SA members are working to ensure that data collected is comparable to other practitioners (please see Section 4.5).

Given the growing body of evidence linking aviation activity to elevated UFP concentrations and the potential health implications, a clear and coordinated approach is essential for addressing this.

As UFP emissions come from a wide range of sources (not just from aviation), we urge the UK Government to define a clear and coordinated path forward for addressing UFPs in the UK. This should include establishing a national framework for UFP monitoring, commissioning research into health impacts, and developing guidance for mitigation strategies. As road transport emissions decline, aviation’s relative contribution to UFPs will increase, making it essential that government policy keeps pace with emerging science and supports industry efforts to improve local air quality.

3.3 Regulatory limits for UFPs

Due to the lack of definitive health impact evidence, there is still no consensus on setting appropriate limit values for exposure to UFPs. The WHO published a “good practice statement” for UFPs (WHO, 2021), with thresholds associated with HIGH and LOW concentrations:

HIGH concentrations: 24-hour mean 10,000 particles/cm3 (24-hour

mean) or 1-hour mean > 20,000 particles/cm3

LOW concentrations: 24-hour mean <1,000 particles/cm3 (24-hour mean)

While these thresholds provide a useful framework for distinguishing between relatively clean and polluted environments, they are not currently realistic targets for most urban areas, where UFP levels routinely exceed the “high” threshold due to dense traffic, industrial activity, and other combustion sources. This highlights the need for context-sensitive approaches to UFP sources. This highlights the need for context-sensitive approaches to UFP management, including improved monitoring, targeted mitigation, and further research into health impacts and exposure pathways.

These thresholds are regularly exceeded across London (Stacey, 2022). Like PM10 and PM2.5, there is technically no health-based limit value below which exposure would be considered safe.

3.4 Emerging research

3.4.1 Emissions Measurement of UFP from Jet Engines

UFPs are hard to measure and require specialist tools to detect.

There is currently no established modelling methodology for environmental dispersion of UFPs, and monitoring of UFPs is not common practice, with only five long-term sites measuring UFP in the UK through Defra’s Particle Concentrations and Numbers Network (DEFRA, 2025).

Various studies have characterised UFP emissions, focusing on non volatile particles, using heated sampling systems. Direct measurement is made difficult due to high temperatures, complex mixing, and large exhaust volumes.

Findings from these studies are summarised below:

Particle Composition is predominantly carbonaceous.

Changing thrust settings will impact the size distribution of particles. This can be seen in the ICAO Emissions Data Bank (ICAO, 2025) where the average particle size changes at different thrust settings.

Different engine types produce varying particle sizes and compositions (ICAO, 2025).

While standardised measurement systems and regulatory limits for non volatile particles have been introduced for aircraft exhaust emissions through the ICAO CAEP 11 regulation, this does not capture the volatile particle emissions which also contribute to the total UFP composition at airports.

The ICAO regulation does not apply to Auxiliary Power Unit emissions, which are also a source of combustion.

3.4.2 Ambient Measurement of UFP at Airports

Studies conducted at various airports including Zurich, Copenhagen, Los Angeles, and Heathrow have identified the following findings:

The particle size distribution of UFPs near airports are smaller than those in urban environments.

Aircraft are recognised as a source of UFP, with higher concentrations

observed during takeoff and landing.

Elevated UFP levels near airports pose potential health risks.

3.4.3 Research Gaps and Future Directions

SA recognises the need for further research in the following areas:

Characterisation: Need for detailed studies on the size, composition, and behaviour of UFP as they disperse from the source, including the volatile component.

Standardisation: Harmonisation of ambient measurement techniques and calibration procedures to ensure data comparability for environmental dispersion.

Health Studies: More research needed to understand the health impacts of UFP exposure near airports.

Climate and atmospheric meteorology: As climate change increases the frequency of extreme heat events, atmospheric stagnation, and heat domes, further research is required to understand how these changing meteorological conditions affect UFP dispersion, secondary particle formation, and localised accumulation around airports.

4. Mitigation Opportunities and Actions

The aviation industry is implementing actions which should reduce UFP emissions. This includes the introduction of SAFs, which have a better air quality footprint than existing fossil fuels, making use of zero emission equipment as airport operations decarbonise, and further exploration of hydrogen and electric aircraft.

Hydrotreating conventional jet fuel also presents some opportunities, however, would require extensive testing. To help address knowledge gaps, SA is sponsoring further research into UFPs at airports.

4.1 Sustainable Aviation Fuel

SAFs, which reduce Greenhouse Gas emissions by 70% on an average lifecycle basis compared to Jet A-1 (Department for Transport, 2024), are one of the key mechanisms to decarbonisation in our 2026 Decarbonisation Road-Map (Sustainable Aviation, 2026).

There is increasing evidence of SAF reducing aviation’s non-CO2 impacts as well as potential for improving local air quality (R. S. Märkl, 2024).

The UK SAF Mandate, which was brought into effect 1 January 2025, and the Revenue Certainty Mechanism, will support a UK SAF production industry. The Mandate requires SAF to make up 2% of jet fuel blends in the UK in 2025, increasing linearly to 10% in 2030 and 22% in 2040.

SAF will be a prevalent focus for decarbonising aviation in the UK and globally. As SAF increases in jet fuel blends, we expect the respective air quality emissions of PM10 and PM2.5 to decrease.

In 2023, Virgin Atlantic led a consortium to deliver the world’s first flight across the Atlantic on 100% SAF to prove the safety of SAF and demonstrate its environmental benefits (Virgin Atlantic, 2024) . The SAF variant used in testing (88% HEFA-SPK, 12% Virent-SAK) used Synthesised Aromatic Kerosene to meet the current fuel specifications. These aromatic compounds are important to ensure compatibility with existing infrastructure but limit the nvPM benefit that can be achieved with low aromatic or zero aromatic SAF. nvPM are one aspect of UFPs.

The ECLIF3 project, involving UK and European partners, investigated the in-flight exhaust and contrail measurements of an Airbus A350 aircraft using 100% HEFA-SPK SAF with very low aromatics. This campaign showed a reduction in both nvPM and total PM at cruise conditions of 22-41%, dependent on the engine power level (Dischl et al., 2024).

Crucially, this reduction in nvPM emissions provides a dual climate and air quality benefit: by decreasing the number of soot particles that act as ice nucleation sites, low-aromatic SAFs reduce contrail ice crystal concentrations, thereby mitigating aviation’s non-CO2 climate warming impact (Märkl et al., 2024) alongside local UFP concentrations.

There are further research projects, ongoing, that are investigating the benefits of SAF such as PACIFIC which is investigating the impact of fuel composition and engine cycle on particle emissions, covering both local air quality and climate impacts using a range of techniques from laboratory tests to full-scale aircraft ground testing (Airbus, 2025).

Within the ICAO Committee on Aviation Environmental Protection (CAEP) work has been completed to develop guidance on predicting the impact that SAF usage has on aircraft engine exhaust emissions. This guidance will be published in an update to Doc 9889: Airport Air Quality Manual. The usage of SAF has a significant impact on both volatile and non-volatile particulate emissions. Because SAF contains virtually no sulphur, it directly eliminates fuel-derived gaseous SOx, thereby suppressing the nucleation of volatile ultrafine sulphate particles in the cooling exhaust plume. Simultaneously, the lower aromatic content of SAF reduces primary non-volatile particle (nvPM) formation during combustion.

For SOx emissions, due to SAF containing no sulphur, the reduction will be dependant solely on the blend ratio of SAF, i.e. a 50% reduction in SOx will be achieved when using a 50% SAF blend. The effect on nvPM mass and number is dependent on the fuel composition as well as the flight phase of the aircraft and the effect will vary for each aircraft/engine combination.

Typically, SAF contains a lower amount of aromatic compounds which results in a higher hydrogen content compared to Jet A-1 fuel leading to a reduction in the formation process of particles. The methodology of predicting non-volatile PM (nvPM) reduction through the use of SAF is therefore based on the change in hydrogen content. This method will be available in the update to the ICAO Airport Air Quality Manual and is also included in Appendix A.

The relationship between SAF and airport UFP levels is less well understood compared to that of SAF and aircraft nvPM emissions. This is one of the research gaps we are looking to address through measures outlined in Section 4.5.

4.2 Decarbonising airfield operations

The impact of reduced fuel burn on the airfield on UFP concentrations has not been modelled or understood. Measures to decarbonise airfields such as electrifying ground service equipment, fixed electrical ground power, pre-conditioned air, single engine taxi, and exploring hydrogen fuel for both aviation and ground support, will also have improvements on local air quality, including UFPs. Measures to reduce emissions from the landing and take-off cycle will also have an impact.

4.3 Hydrogen and electric aircraft

Our 2026 Decarbonisation Road-Map includes hydrogen and electric aircraft as part of the path to net zero. These technologies are areas of active research and development and will potentially provide benefits to LAQ once implemented as hydrogen powered aircraft, whether through combustion of hydrogen or hydrogen fuel cell, and electric aircraft will not produce any UFPs.

4.4 Hydrotreating conventional jet fuel

Improving conventional jet fuel quality alongside increasing levels of SAF is the most direct and scalable way the aviation industry can reduce UFP emissions. Conventional jet fuels can contain high aromatic and sulphur content due to the variable nature of global production.

One effective solution is hydrotreating, a refining process that removes aromatics and sulphur from jet fuel, resulting in lower particulate emissions. While a minimum level of aromatics is still required for compatibility with certain components, such as nitrile seals, fuel gauging systems and auto-ignition parameters, this constraint is less relevant for modern aircraft and fuel systems which are designed to operate safely with low-aromatic or aromatic-free fuels, though it should be noted that some SAFs may contain higher aromatic content than conventional jet.

However, any strategic recommendations regarding hydrotreating must carefully balance local air quality improvements against wider climate considerations. The additional processing required during hydrotreating increases refinery energy demand, which could impact upstream lifecycle greenhouse gas emissions. Furthermore, reducing sulphur and aromatic content involves complex non-CO2 atmospheric trade-offs, including changes to aerosol radiative forcing. Consequently, the net climate impact must be fully evaluated alongside air quality benefits.

By phasing out legacy components and undertaking modifications with

associated costs to be compatible with low aromatics, the sector can unlock substantial air quality and climate benefits. As with the use of 100% SAF with low or zero aromatics, extensive testing will be required to ensure compatibility with existing aircraft as well as regulation and infrastructure changes before the full benefit of hydrotreating can be achieved.

4.5 Addressing research gaps

The measurement of UFPs and the impact of aviation on UFP concentration pathways and patterns is important to SA members. To address knowledge gaps on this topic, SA has sponsored a PhD student at the University of Birmingham. This PhD will run until 2031 and will address:

Measurement Technology

◦ Size range

◦ Suitability

◦ Calibration

◦ Co-location studies

Particle Characteristics

◦ Size from 0.5nm

◦ Composition of volatile and non-volatile fractions

◦ Behaviour of particles as they disperse downwind of exhaust

Impact on UFP levels from SAF

SA is supporting the PhD through funding, access to data and sites for data capture, and funding additional equipment as needed. Airport members are collaborating in a co-ordinated approach to support the PhD to give a view of the variety of airport locations and fleets across the UK.

4.5.1 Further Opportunities

The research outlined in Section 4.5 will deepen the industry’s understanding of UFP concentrations and dispersion patterns around airports. There is opportunity for regulatory standards to guide further measurement of UFPs across all known sources, including road which would greatly improve knowledge of UFP concentrations.

5. Summary

Sustainable Aviation is committed to understanding the impacts of UFPs and to mitigating risks to local air quality. This paper outlines our current understanding of UFPs, the potential opportunities to mitigate these impacts, and provides an overview of some of the work that the aviation industry is doing to mitigate these impacts and advance knowledge and understanding.

Crucially, while we actively support transparent evidence-gathering, policy frameworks must recognise that setting binding regulatory limits or operational mandates at this stage would be premature relative to the current state of science and technological maturity.

Sustainable Aviation will keep this topic under active review, continuing to support research that strengthens the evidence base so that any future policy or operational measures remain grounded in robust, validated science. As our understanding of UFPs improves, we will act to mitigate any outcomes accordingly.

As Canadian oil sands cutbacks squeeze conventional refiners, XCF Global demonstrates how domestic waste-to-fuel production insulates transportation fuel supplies from cross-border disruptions.

XCF Global Inc. (“XCF”) (NASDAQ:SAFX), a scaling U.S.-based producer of renewable diesel and sustainable aviation fuel (“SAF”), today addressed current dynamics across North American fuel markets as U.S. refiners face tighter crude slates following recent production pullbacks and maintenance across Canadian oil sands facilities.

Because Canadian heavy crude is a primary feedstock for North American diesel production, supply reductions create direct margin pressure and output bottlenecks for traditional refining infrastructure. XCF Global’s production model, anchored by its flagship New Rise Renewables Reno facility, operates entirely outside the petroleum crude supply chain, converting domestic agricultural and waste byproducts directly into drop-in distillates.

Key Strategic Advantages During Conventional Supply Squeezes:

Crude-Free Feedstock Independence: Unlike petroleum refiners tied to pipeline flows and heavy crude price spreads, XCF utilizes domestic waste streams (such as distillers corn oil) that are not impacted by geopolitical crude disruptions.

Drop-In Middle Distillate Relief: Renewable diesel functions as a direct, seamless replacement for petroleum diesel across commercial fleets, municipal transport, and industrial distribution without requiring engine modifications or new dispensing infrastructure.

Commercial Momentum: Building on its daily commercial delivery pace at the New Rise Reno facility, XCF continues to advance its operational throughput toward its permitted nameplate capacity of up to 38 million gallons per year.

“Whenever cross-border crude pipelines or oil sands extraction face downtime, conventional refiners feel an immediate squeeze in their middle distillate output,” said Chris Cooper, Chief Executive Officer of XCF Global. “XCF Global was built to solve this exact vulnerability. By refining domestic, waste-based feedstocks right here in the U.S., we deliver stable, commercial-scale renewable diesel while staying focused on scaling production where feedstock supply and customer demand are best aligned. That approach helps protect commercial fuel buyers from crude market shocks while supporting alternative lower emissions fuels.”

XCF believes its domestic, waste-based production model can support greater fuel supply resilience while providing a lower-carbon pathway for middle distillate production.

text:
EVA Air, AIT Worldwide Logistics and Microsoft are launching a two-year program to use sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) produced from used cooking oil. In the first year, the project is expected to deliver around 15 thsd tons of CO₂ emissions reductions across Microsoft’s supply chain.

The SAF will be produced by Taiwan’s Formosa Petrochemical from used cooking oil. Both the feedstock and production process are certified under the ISCC system. According to the companies, the fuel can reduce lifecycle greenhouse gas emissions by around 80% compared with conventional jet fuel.

EVA Air will provide Microsoft with SAF environmental attributes linked to flights departing Taiwan. This will allow the technology company to account for Scope 3 emissions reductions associated with air freight transportation of equipment for its cloud infrastructure.

SAF use has already become part of EVA Air’s long-term strategy. The airline has been using sustainable aviation fuel on flights departing Asia, Europe and North America since 2025 and has also signed a five-year SAF procurement agreement with Formosa Petrochemical.

The expansion of SAF is creating additional demand for used vegetable oils, which are among the main feedstocks for producing this fuel through the HEFA pathway. Platts assessed SAF HEFA-SPK FOB Straits at $2,487.25 per ton on August 25, down $10 from the previous day.

title: Renewable Propane Making Path to Zero Easier for Ports
description:

That’s why Stewart said working with a propane provider with experience in renewable propane is a must.
text:
With increasing supply, ultra-low-carbon fuel will be a ‘game changer’

Propane, with its low carbon content and much lower harmful emissions than diesel and gasoline, has become a key tool for decarbonization and cleaner air around many of the United States’ more than 300 ports. From terminal tractors to up to Class 7 forklifts to generators and light- and medium-duty vehicles, propane-powered equipment is a good fit at both seaports and inland ports. Looking ahead to an even greener future, the next step in decarbonization for these key facilitators of American economic growth is renewable propane. As progress continues on ports’ path to zero carbon emissions, developments in renewable propane are poised to provide a big boost.

Renewable propane is molecularly identical to conventional propane, and is made from a variety of feedstocks, including camelina seed oil, vegetable oil, animal fats, and used cooking oil. It is a drop-in replacement for conventional propane, meaning customers can use renewable propane without additional infrastructure or costly new equipment.

That’s why propane providers like Jeff Stewart, president of Blue Star Gas in Santa Rosa, California, are bullish about renewable propane. Blue Star Gas is located in the state with two of the largest and busiest ports in America, the Port of Los Angeles and the Port of Long Beach, and a state with aggressive goals for decarbonization. For Blue Star Gas’s customers, Stewart says renewable propane will be “a dramatic game changer” as supply continues to increase.

Increasing capacity of renewable propane

According to the U.S. Department of Energy Alternative Fuels Data Center, U.S. renewable propane production capacity is more than 4.5 million gallons per year. Stewart said that number is bound to increase, and perhaps significantly. The World Liquid Gas Association adds that renewable propane could meet half of the world’s propane demand by 2050. With propane distribution infrastructure already in place, it will be easy for ports of all sizes to adopt renewable propane.

“It’s not difficult to get renewable propane physically to a port,” he said. “It uses the same exact infrastructure as conventional propane. The challenge at this point is really in the volume and production. But we are starting to see new producers coming into the marketplace, and as the volume grows, there will be more supply available for ports.”

According to Stewart, renewable propane in the marketplace today is primarily a byproduct of the refining process for renewable diesel and sustainable aviation fuel. While a good portion of renewable propane is generated at a refinery in Louisiana, refineries in California have recently become bio-refineries, and they aren’t using any crude-based feedstock.

Stewart reports that 20 percent of Blue Star’s volume is renewable propane Autogas — a form of propane used in vehicle applications and material handling. At the port, material handling remains the primary focus.

Progressing toward zero emissions with renewable propane

The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) Ports Initiative is an incentive-based program designed to reduce emissions by encouraging port authorities and terminal operators to retrofit and replace older diesel engines with new technologies and use cleaner fuels, such as conventional and renewable propane.

Renewable propane has a carbon intensity score of between 20 and 43. This compares to 80 for conventional propane and natural gas, both of which are 20% cleaner than gasoline and diesel (both 100). At 130, the average score of the U.S. electrical grid is the highest among all options.

Because renewable propane offers the same reliability and power as conventional propane, it can dramatically accelerate a port’s progress toward decarbonization while still being able to run efficient operations and meet tight deadlines for tasks like offloading ships.

For ports that want to step into the realm of renewable propane, which is typically blended with conventional propane, the process should be planned and calculated. That’s why Stewart said working with a propane provider with experience in renewable propane is a must.

“If you want to start a trial, that trial can be supported right now,” he said. “Depending on the volume and the eventual rollout, I think it will line up with the growth of the product.”
