title: For the time being, biochar can be more cost-effective than sustainable aviation fuel.
description:
With sustainable aviation fuel, usually referred to as SAF in the industry, it is converted into a liquid fuel that replaces fossil kerosene.
What the comparison yields For biochar, the average comes out at approximately 177 dollars per ton of CO2.
For aviation fuel from residual and waste streams, that figure is around 448 dollars, so more than twice as high.
Clearly more expensive are the routes that produce aviation fuel from alcohol, at 938 dollars, and the route via rapid pyrolysis, at 652 dollars.
Those who sequester CO2 receive certificates at the project level, while those who supply fuel use aviation life cycle standards.
text:
Residual streams from forests, agriculture, and households now have numerous applications, ranging from green gas and heat to bio-based chemistry and materials. Two of these yield climate benefits in fundamentally different ways. With biochar, the material is heated without oxygen, resulting in a carbon-rich product that is applied to the soil, where the carbon remains for a long time instead of being released into the air as CO2. With sustainable aviation fuel, usually referred to as SAF in the industry, it is converted into a liquid fuel that replaces fossil kerosene. The first route removes carbon from the cycle; the second prevents the addition of new fossil carbon. It is precisely this difference that makes the two difficult to compare side by side.

Yet that is precisely what three researchers did in the open-access journal iScience, in an article published on August 21, 2026. Hassan El-Houjeiri of the KAPSARC research institute in Riyadh, Adam Brandt of Stanford University, and Mohammad Masnadi of the University of Pittsburgh deliberately focused on these two routes. Biomass is a scarce commodity with limitations regarding moisture content, energy density, and supply, they argue, and therefore its value is best realized in sectors where hardly any alternatives exist. Aviation is the prime example of this. Moreover, there are enough published cost studies on both routes to build a comparison. Other applications of residual streams fall outside their analysis.

What was missing until now was a way to make those studies comparable, the authors write. They converted everything to 2024 dollars and applied the same yardstick: what does it cost to remove one ton of CO2 from the air or keep it out? The research received no external funding, and the authors report no conflicts of interest.

What the comparison yields

For biochar, the average comes out at approximately 177 dollars per ton of CO2. For aviation fuel from residual and waste streams, that figure is around 448 dollars, so more than twice as high. For biochar, the most known cases range between 111 and 497 dollars. For SAF, the spread is much wider, from 98 to 948 dollars, and this is because very different techniques fall under that single umbrella.

These techniques are worth examining, as they differ significantly. The only route currently operating commercially on a large scale uses waste fats and oils and is called HEFA. This comes in at around 362 dollars per ton of CO2. Gasification followed by Fischer-Tropsch synthesis comes close to that at 342 dollars. Clearly more expensive are the routes that produce aviation fuel from alcohol, at 938 dollars, and the route via rapid pyrolysis, at 652 dollars. Precisely these more expensive routes are necessary to ever achieve large volumes, because there is simply not enough waste fat in the world. The researchers do note, however, that they could only find three and two public cases for those two, respectively—too few to base firm conclusions on.

The substantiation for biochar is more robust. The researchers used seventeen cost studies and also examined nineteen installations included in the Puro.earth certification register. Such installations are required to have verified how much CO2 they actually sequester, after deducting the emissions from collection and processing itself. This turned out to lie between 0,9 and 3,2 tonnes of CO2 per ton of biochar. Scale makes a significant difference here: an installation producing ten times as much does so at nearly sixty percent lower costs per ton. That gain has its limits, however, because beyond a certain scale, raw materials must be sourced from increasingly further afield. The researchers were unable to substantiate exactly where that tipping point lies with figures.

Not a choice, but an order

The main message of the study is not that biochar wins. The authors state in so many words that their outcome is not a prescription for where residual streams should go. That depends on what is available locally, who else lays claim to it, what subsidies are available, and what infrastructure is already in place. Moreover, they point out that biochar itself is part of a broader family of options for capturing carbon from biomass, and that some of these can prove cheaper or more sustainable in certain situations. Furthermore, the additional benefits of both routes, such as the soil activity of biochar or the contribution of SAF to one's own fuel supply, were not included in the cost comparison.

What the authors do point out is a difference in timing. Biochar is a mature technology that is already operational, accounting for an estimated global production capacity of more than 350 kilotons per year in 2023, spread across six continents. For the period up to approximately 2030, that is the route that can scale up rapidly. Aviation fuel from woody residues and household waste would only really start to matter in the 2030s and 2040s, and then only if the first factories of that type prove to operate reliably. That is not a given. The researchers point to a series of projects that were delayed, restructured, or failed altogether.

The current figures underscore how nascent that market still is. In 2025, around 2 million tonnes of SAF were produced worldwide, approximately 0,7 percent of all kerosene consumed by aircraft. In its forecast for 2050, aviation umbrella organization IATA assumes that waste fats and oils will supply slightly more than fifteen percent of SAF by then, agroforestry residues about a quarter, and household residual waste about seven percent.

For policymakers, there is another catch. Blending obligations, tax benefits, and purchasing agreements with airlines can push biomass towards fuel, even if sequestration per ton of CO2 is cheaper. Moreover, the two certification systems operate independently of each other. Those who sequester CO2 receive certificates at the project level, while those who supply fuel use aviation life cycle standards. As soon as the same raw material is listed in both systems, double counting is a real risk.

The researchers themselves call their study a snapshot and not a definitive ranking of biomass routes. Better operational data from SAF plants running on woody residues could still shift the picture.

title: Zero Petroleum eyes commercial plant after replicating Jet A-1 with green hydrogen
description:
UK start-up Zero Petroleum is working on its first commercial-scale plant after claiming to have proven the chemistry of a green hydrogen-based 100% replica of A-1 jet fuel.
It was produced at the firm’s pre-commercial Plant Zero.1 facility near Oxford, which features direct air capture equipment for CO2 sourcing, an electrolyser powered by solar energy for green hydrogen, and the company’s DirectFT synthesis platform.
Jet A-1 is particularly difficult to reproduce because it is a mixture of hundreds of hydrocarbons to balance more than 70 chemical and physical properties, including density, freezing point, viscosity, thermal stability, and electrical characteristics.
Many SAF production methods make fuels that lack some of the components found in fossil jet fuel, meaning they may burn similarly but behave differently in aircraft fuel systems.

text:
UK start-up Zero Petroleum is working on its first commercial-scale plant after claiming to have proven the chemistry of a green hydrogen-based 100% replica of A-1 jet fuel.

The undisclosed facility recently had a pre-front-end engineering design (FEED) completed by Technip Energies and will produce a synthetic fuel Zero Petroleum claims could be used as the sole propellant for jet-engined aircraft.

According to the company, the sustainable aviation fuel (SAF), created by combining green hydrogen and carbon dioxide (CO2) through Zero Petroleum’s Fischer-Tropsch synthesis process at its Oxford research facility, could eliminate the 50% blending limit applied to most SAF.

It was produced at the firm’s pre-commercial Plant Zero.1 facility near Oxford, which features direct air capture equipment for CO2 sourcing, an electrolyser powered by solar energy for green hydrogen, and the company’s DirectFT synthesis platform.

Jet A-1 is particularly difficult to reproduce because it is a mixture of hundreds of hydrocarbons to balance more than 70 chemical and physical properties, including density, freezing point, viscosity, thermal stability, and electrical characteristics.

Many SAF production methods make fuels that lack some of the components found in fossil jet fuel, meaning they may burn similarly but behave differently in aircraft fuel systems.

The company said testing by assurance firm Intertek confirmed the major properties of its synthetic fuel fell within the ranges found in conventional Jet A-1.

Work on the fuel was backed by the UK SAF Clearing House, and the new facility’s pre-FEED benefitted from £3.5m ($4.1m) awarded through the Department for Transport’s (DFT) Advanced Fuels Fund grant.

While Zero Petroleum did not outline a timeline for the site’s construction, it said it is now “poised for commercial scale-up.”

It comes as the UK’s hydrogen aviation sector continues to garner steady public and private support as innovators strive to facilitate meeting UK SAF mandates dictating 10% of jet fuel supplied to the UK aviation market to be sustainable by 2030.

text:
Massive cargo ships that run on green methanol are now sailing scheduled routes, and ports and suppliers are organizing the infrastructure to fuel them.

In July, the world’s largest methanol dual-fuel container cargo ship, the 400-meter-long OOCL Wisdom, completed its first green methanol fueling (or “bunkering”) at China’s Qingdao Port. Days later, Dutch terminal operator VTTI completed its first large-scale green methanol bunkering load at its facility in Dalian, China. On 11 July, 20 organizations spanning shipping, ports, energy, and equipment manufacturing launched a Methanol Fuel Shipping Supply Chain Innovation Alliance to coordinate a national bunkering buildout.

Methanol fuel for shipping barely exists as an industry today. Yet if the global shipping fleet fully converts to methanol fuel, the industry’s annual methanol demand could reach 100 million tons a year by 2050, according to a National Center for Energy Analytics projection. That raises the question the industry has been dancing around for years—where is all that methanol supposed to come from?

For most of the previous century, making methanol meant building a colossal, centralized plant near a cheap natural-gas supply. A new wave of startups is betting that the old formula is backwards for the low-carbon methanol needed for shipping. Instead of piping stranded methane to a plant, the new idea holds, it’s cheaper to bring a plant to the methane.

Today, Emvolon—an MIT spinout founded in 2021 by Emmanuel Kasseris and Leslie Bromberg—announced the details of an agreement to sell up to US $450 million of the company’s biomethanol and other liquid fuels over a seven-year period to Stamford, Connecticut-based commodities trader Freepoint Commodities. Kasseris says the deal will fund construction of Emvolon’s fleet of modular, container-size plants, which convert methane from landfills and other waste sites directly into ship fuel.

Engine-Based Syngas Methanol Production

Rather than engineering a conventional chemical reformer, Emvolon repurposes an off-the-shelf automotive engine to help produce methanol. Emvolon runs the engine “fuel rich” (meaning more fuel is injected into the cylinders than can be burned with the amount of air in the mix). As a result, the cylinders produce syngas—a mix of carbon monoxide and hydrogen—instead of burning methane all the way to carbon dioxide and water. Syngas is then synthesized into methanol. Kasseris says the approach cuts the capital cost of small-scale chemical production by an order of magnitude compared with a purpose-built reformer.

Each complete system is roughly container-sized and converts about 3,500 cubic meters of methane into 8 tons of methanol a day. Trucked to a landfill, wastewater plant, or flare stack, it turns a gas stream that would otherwise be vented or burned into a liquid fuel that leaves by ordinary tanker truck—no new pipeline required.

A metal box that looks like an ordinary shipping container on the outside could contain machinery that converts the methane emitted by landfills and oil wells into green methanol. Emvolon

Emvolon has already moved from lab demonstration to commercial deployment. The company’s first commercial reformer is going up at a landfill in Humble, Texas, near Houston’s Bush Intercontinental Airport under a joint venture Emvolon and Montauk Renewables signed in 2025. The unit will run at roughly half a ton to a ton of methanol per day to start, Kasseris says, and Emvolon is targeting production to begin in 2027.

Emvolon isn’t limited to projects it develops itself. A landfill or gas-site owner could buy units outright and arrange separate offtake agreements for the produced methanol, Kasseris says. Emvolon can offer anything from equipment and training alone up to a full package of hardware, offtake, and financing—though he expects the company will eventually specialize in one side of that business as it scales.

A Growing Fleet of Methanol-Fueled Ships

Kasseris puts the current count of methanol-capable ships on order or in operation at roughly 400—evidence, in his view, of demand that’s already here. Ships calling at European ports already face the EU’s Emissions Trading System and FuelEU Maritime rules, which price a vessel’s carbon intensity and push shipowners toward cleaner fuel. Kasseris expects Chinese policy to move the same direction; July’s alliance launch and the Maritime Technologies Forum‘s new methanol safety guidelines suggest the regulatory scaffolding is catching up to the hardware.

In addition to being environmentally friendly, green methanol scores points for practicality. It’s liquid at room temperature, easier to store than hydrogen or ammonia, and simpler to synthesize than long-chain synthetic hydrocarbons. Kasseris also notes that methanol isn’t a one-market bet; gasoline blending, industrial buyers, and eventually sustainable aviation fuel can all draw on the same supply.

The modular, at-the-source approach has been gaining adherents for years. WasteFuel, a Los Angeles-based waste-to-fuel developer, introduced a containerized “Methanol Module” in 2022 and has an offtake agreement with Maersk for 30,000 tons of bio-methanol annually. Maverick Synfuels, based in North Carolina’s Research Triangle, has marketed small, co-located gas-to-liquids plants since 2014. Houston-based HyOrc and engineering firm Re:Build Optimation are pursuing similar builds. WasteFuel, Maverick, and HyOrc did not respond to requests for comment from IEEE Spectrum.

WOBURN, Mass. and STAMFORD, Conn., Aug. 27, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Emvolon, Inc. (Emvolon), an MIT-spinout commercializing technology that converts methane-rich waste gases into high-value liquid fuels, and Freepoint Commodities LLC (Freepoint), a leading global physical commodity merchant, today announced the execution of two definitive commercial agreements. The transaction establishes Freepoint as both the anchor off-taker and a cornerstone project capital partner across Emvolon’s global deployment pipeline.

Under a seven-year Commodity Purchase Framework Agreement, Freepoint will serve as the primary buyer for biomethanol and associated liquid fuels produced across Emvolon’s deployment sites. Production volumes are structured to scale toward 300,000 metric tons annually as Emvolon’s portfolio expands, delivering commercial-scale fuel directly into Freepoint’s global physical distribution network.

In a concurrent financial agreement, Freepoint has secured direct co-investment participation rights to deploy equity and debt capital across Emvolon’s project portfolio and clean energy infrastructure assets. This balance-sheet backing bridges the gap between technology deployment and long-term project debt financing, providing waste asset operators, such as landfills, dairy farms, and industrial gas sites with a fully de-risked, turnkey fuel production solution.

“Energy security and supply chain resilience and sustainability dictate that we produce essential liquid fuels locally using domestic waste resources that are currently flared or lost,” said Emmanuel Kasseris, Ph.D., Co-Founder and CEO of Emvolon. “This dual commercial and capital agreement with Freepoint systematically solves the core bottleneck in decentralized fuel manufacturing by securing our buyer and anchoring our project financing platform. We are building our first commercial system now and will put that foundation to work across North America and key international growth regions.”

A Replicable "Fuels-as-a-Service" Blueprint for Global Expansion

Rather than operating as a passive technology licensor, Emvolon delivers a turnkey "Liquid Fuels-as-a-Service" platform that systematically eliminates execution risk for waste gas site owners. Emvolon’s commercial template aligns three essential pillars:

Site & Feedstock Development: Partnering with premier waste operators to secure stranded methane streams, as demonstrated by Emvolon's joint venture with Montauk Renewables.

Modular Conversion Technology: Deploying modular micro-reactors that repurpose mass-produced automotive engines to convert waste gas directly into liquid fuels on-site, bypassing grid and pipeline constraints.

Offtake, Logistics & Capital: Partnering with Freepoint to ensure product offtake, manage global distribution, and provide balance-sheet capital at the individual project level.

This standardized, plug-and-play template enables Emvolon to flexibly replicate projects across target regions, including landfill, agricultural, and industrial gas resource bases in North America and other regions, without custom engineering delays or regional infrastructure bottlenecks.

“Freepoint is focused on building resilient commodity supply chains and identifying proprietary technologies capable of scaling rapidly to meet physical supply deficits,” said Mark Lay, Managing Director at Freepoint. “Emvolon’s modular deployment model offers a practical solution to localized fuel production. Our dual commercial and capital commitment reflects our commitment to renewable chemicals and fuels.”

Capitalizing on Premium $1,000/Ton Commodity Demand

Methanol represents a $40 billion annual and rapidly-growing global market with diversified commercial applications across maritime shipping, heavy transport, specialty chemicals, and newly approved Methanol-to-Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF) production pathways. Driven by global supply deficits for cost-competitive low-carbon fuels, RED-II-compliant biomethanol is trading at a premium exceeding $1,000 per metric ton. By producing low-cost liquid commodities directly at emission sites, Emvolon's modular economics deliver attractive commercial margins independent of shifting policy environments.

Founded in 2011, Freepoint is based in Stamford, Connecticut, and employs more than 600 people worldwide. The company is a global merchant of physical commodities, providing customers with physical supply and logistics chain management and services, along with environmentally friendly products and solutions. www.freepoint.com

Emvolon’s patented technology platform converts waste gases from landfills, dairies, wastewater treatment facilities, and industrial flare gas into sustainable fuels and chemicals, including methanol, at the source of waste. title: Adams Land & Cattle breaks ground on $300 million renewable natural gas project
description:
Manure from one of Nebraska’s largest cattle-feeding operations will soon be used to produce renewable natural gas as Adams Land & Cattle breaks ground on a $300 million project south of Broken Bow.
The renewable natural gas facility will use eight anaerobic digesters and is expected to produce about 1.2 million MMBtu of pipeline-quality renewable natural gas annually, according to the companies.

text:
Manure from one of Nebraska’s largest cattle-feeding operations will soon be used to produce renewable natural gas as Adams Land & Cattle breaks ground on a $300 million project south of Broken Bow.

The Broken Bow-based cattle feeder is partnering with Neogenyx Fuels to build an anaerobic digestion facility that will convert cattle manure into pipeline-quality renewable natural gas.

Adams Land & Cattle CEO Abram Babcock said the project represents a new way to capture value from a byproduct the feedlot has long had to manage.

“It’s something we’ve had to manage. It’s a byproduct,” Babcock said in an interview. “We can extract and capture the gas and generate revenue.”

The project is being built alongside a major renovation of the Adams feedlot, including the use of roller-compacted concrete.

The renewable natural gas facility will use eight anaerobic digesters and is expected to produce about 1.2 million MMBtu of pipeline-quality renewable natural gas annually, according to the companies. It is expected to avoid up to 63,700 metric tons of carbon dioxide emissions each year.

The gas will be processed to meet pipeline specifications, allowing it to be injected into existing natural gas infrastructure.

Mike Bakas, CEO of Neogenyx Fuels, said that creates potential markets well beyond Nebraska, including the international maritime industry.

“This product is essentially, when we’re done, the same constituency of natural gas,” Bakas said. “We have to meet a specification set by the pipeline company to be able to inject our gas into the pipeline.”

Bakas said renewable natural gas produced from the cattle manure could eventually be converted to liquefied natural gas for use as a lower-carbon marine fuel.

The project also is designed to recover additional products from the manure.

A screw press will separate a fibrous material that Adams plans to use for cattle bedding. A centrifuge will separate nutrients into concentrated phosphorus and nitrogen fertilizer products.

Babcock said the process will allow the operation to retain the phosphorus and nitrogen that are valuable to farmers while producing a more concentrated fertilizer product.

Neogenyx also expects to capture biogenic carbon dioxide from the process. Bakas said that nearly pure stream of carbon dioxide could potentially be used for industrial purposes or, with additional processing, beverage-grade applications.

The companies describe the project as an early example of pairing a large cattle-feeding operation with renewable fuel production.

“This is a way that we can continue to leverage rural America to help with that production,” Babcock said.

Babcock said the project represents a significant investment in Broken Bow and Custer County. He said the partnership is expected to continue for at least 25 years.

The project is also expected to create more than 100 construction jobs and about 20 permanent operational jobs, according to Neogenyx.

Nebraska Gov. Jim Pillen, who attended the groundbreaking, called it a major day for Broken Bow and Nebraska agriculture.

“Nebraska’s growing some food, and now we’re energy,” Pillen said.

U.S. Sen. Pete Ricketts said the project demonstrates how agricultural waste can become part of the nation’s energy supply.

“Agriculture is the heart of what we do, and we want to create more value added agriculture. And this project brings together two key ones livestock and biofuels. And by taking the manure off the cattle and turning it into renewable natural gas, we’re adding to American energy dominance. We’re making it so we bring our energy prices down,” Ricketts said in an interview.

Ricketts said renewable natural gas adds another value-added opportunity for Nebraska agriculture, alongside ethanol, biodiesel, renewable diesel and the developing sustainable aviation fuel industry.

For Adams Land & Cattle, Babcock said the renewable energy project also creates possibilities for a more integrated cattle-feeding operation.

“We just have a lot of opportunities,” he said.

The renewable natural gas facility is Neogenyx Fuels’ first agricultural anaerobic digester project. The company will own and operate the facility, while Adams Land & Cattle will provide the manure and handle the nutrient products produced by the process.

The companies expect the facility to demonstrate how livestock agriculture can participate in emerging energy markets while creating new revenue streams in rural communities.

As Canadian oil sands cutbacks squeeze conventional refiners, XCF Global demonstrates how domestic waste-to-fuel production insulates transportation fuel supplies from cross-border disruptions.

("XCF") (NASDAQ: SAFX), a scaling U.S.-based producer of renewable diesel and sustainable aviation fuel ("SAF"), today addressed current dynamics across North American fuel markets as U.S. refiners face tighter crude slates following recent production pullbacks and maintenance across Canadian oil sands facilities.

Because Canadian heavy crude is a primary feedstock for North American diesel production, supply reductions create direct margin pressure and output bottlenecks for traditional refining infrastructure. XCF Global's production model, anchored by its flagship New Rise Renewables Reno facility, operates entirely outside the petroleum crude supply chain, converting domestic agricultural and waste byproducts directly into drop-in distillates.

Key Strategic Advantages During Conventional Supply Squeezes:

Crude-Free Feedstock Independence: Unlike petroleum refiners tied to pipeline flows and heavy crude price spreads, XCF utilizes domestic waste streams (such as distillers corn oil) that are not impacted by geopolitical crude disruptions.

Drop-In Middle Distillate Relief: Renewable diesel functions as a direct, seamless replacement for petroleum diesel across commercial fleets, municipal transport, and industrial distribution without requiring engine modifications or new dispensing infrastructure.

Commercial Momentum: Building on its daily commercial delivery pace at the New Rise Reno facility, XCF continues to advance its operational throughput toward its permitted nameplate capacity of up to 38 million gallons per year.

"Whenever cross-border crude pipelines or oil sands extraction face downtime, conventional refiners feel an immediate squeeze in their middle distillate output," said Chris Cooper, Chief Executive Officer of XCF Global. "XCF Global was built to solve this exact vulnerability. By refining domestic, waste-based feedstocks right here in the U.S., we deliver stable, commercial-scale renewable diesel while staying focused on scaling production where feedstock supply and customer demand are best aligned. That approach helps protect commercial fuel buyers from crude market shocks while supporting alternative lower emissions fuels."

XCF believes its domestic, waste-based production model can support greater fuel supply resilience while providing a lower-carbon pathway for middle distillate production.

text:
Strengthening Commitment to Sustainable Aviation

EVA Air, in collaboration with the American Institute in Taiwan (AIT) and Microsoft, has announced an expansion of its sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) initiative, reinforcing efforts to reduce the carbon footprint of air transportation. This partnership will see flights departing from Taiwan utilizing SAF supplied by Formosa Petrochemical Corporation (FPCC). The fuel is derived from used cooking oil (UCO) and certified under the International Sustainability and Carbon Certification (ISCC) system, which ensures that both the feedstock and production processes adhere to stringent sustainability criteria.

Clay Sun, President of EVA Air, emphasized the importance of cross-sector collaboration in achieving net-zero aviation. He noted that aligning customer demand with industry capabilities can accelerate the development of the SAF market, and expressed optimism about expanding partnerships to establish lower-carbon air transportation as a global supply chain standard.

Environmental Impact and Corporate Responsibility

Sustainable aviation fuel offers a significant environmental advantage, reducing lifecycle greenhouse gas emissions by approximately 80% compared to conventional jet fuel. The environmental benefits of the SAF used in this initiative will be tracked and retired through the ISCC Credit Transfer System (CTS), an internationally recognized registry that monitors sustainability attributes. This mechanism allows Microsoft to account for Scope 3 emissions reductions associated with its air freight operations, reflecting a broader corporate trend toward addressing indirect emissions within supply chains.

Microsoft’s participation is expected to stimulate increased corporate demand for SAF, potentially encouraging wider adoption across the aviation industry and further emissions reductions. As companies intensify efforts to lower their carbon footprints, investor interest in sustainable aviation initiatives is likely to grow. This dynamic may prompt competitors to enhance their own SAF strategies or pursue similar partnerships to maintain market relevance.

Challenges and Future Outlook

Despite the positive momentum, the expansion of sustainable aviation fuel faces notable challenges. High initial production costs, logistical complexities in scaling supply, and the need to navigate regulatory frameworks across different jurisdictions remain significant obstacles. Overcoming these issues will require sustained cooperation among airlines, fuel producers, policymakers, and corporate customers.

The partnership between EVA Air, AIT, and Microsoft underscores both the potential and the difficulties inherent in transitioning to sustainable aviation. By aligning customer demand with industry resources, the initiative seeks to establish a new benchmark for lower-carbon air transportation within global supply chains.

text:
KROHNE has been highlighting its process instrumentation portfolio engineered for the sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) market.

The portfolio enables producers to manage challenging feedstocks, hydrogen service and demanding process conditions ranging from pretreatment through the final downstream process.

As SAF projects move from first-of-a-kind plants toward larger-scale deployment, engineers are under pressure to upscale the process while maintaining reliable, economically viable production assets.

“The SAF industry brings together two very different worlds,” said Yannick Farine, industry manager biofuels and bioenergy at KROHNE.

“Success depends on understanding the behavior of renewable feedstocks upstream while also meeting the demands of downstream refining. Our goal is to help customers optimise processes, reduce maintenance and build SAF plants they can rely on for years to come.”

A central element of this concept is the wider use of ultrasonic flowmeters in SAF service. Unlike many traditional technologies, ultrasonic flowmeters have no internal restrictions, capillaries or moving parts and are well suited to abrasive feedstocks, hydrogen-rich streams, high-pressure steam and other critical services.

Their ability to operate at temperatures up to 600C and at high pressures for both liquids and gases makes them one of the few technologies capable of delivering accurate measurement across a broad envelope of SAF conditions.

Advanced noise-filtering in ultrasonic gas flowmeters also supports reliable hydrogen measurement, which can be challenging due to the gas’s high velocity of sound and demanding operating environment.

Global law firm Clifford Chance has advised the lenders on the financing of Egypt's first sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) production facility.

The project marks the development of the first project-financed SAF plant in Africa and the Middle East.

The $212.4 million (£181 million) project is supported by a $142.9 million (£122 million) debt package provided by The Arab Energy Fund (TAEF), Qatar National Bank (QNB) and The Emerging Africa & Asia Infrastructure Fund and Emerging Markets Transition Debt Fund, funds managed by Ninety One.

Shell will act as the plant's primary feedstock provider and sole offtaker, pursuant to a long-term take-or-pay offtake agreement, supporting the project's long-term commercial viability. Axens will provide its proprietary processing technology.

Located in the Sokhna Special Economic Zone in Egypt, the project is being developed with the support of sponsors Green Sky Capital Management, Al Mana Holding and Vision Invest.

The facility is designed to produce 200,000 tonnes per annum of biofuels, including SAF and other green products and will utilise Hydroprocessed Esters and Fatty Acids (HEFA) technology to convert waste-based feedstock into high-grade sustainable fuel.

Nicholas Wong, partner, commented: " This financing demonstrates how we are helping to bring together the right combination of lenders and commercial arrangements to support the development of SAF infrastructure and establish a bankable model for future projects in the region.”

Tom Capel, counsel, added: " As the first project-financed SAF facility in the region, this project sets important precedents, deepens the market's understanding of how SAF infrastructure can be developed and financed, and builds confidence across the sector. Transactions such as this demonstrate how the right combination of stakeholders can come together and execute meaningful energy transition projects at scale and with efficiency."

description:
EVA Air has signed an MOU with freight forwarder AIT Worldwide Logistics to expand its Green Transportation Program over the next two years.
We look forward to working with more partners to make lower-carbon air transportation the new standard for global supply chains."
In comparison to conventional jet fuel, SAF delivers approximately 80% lower lifecycle greenhouse gas emissions.
Through its Green Transportation Program, EVA Air helps corporate customers and freight forwarders better understand the carbon footprint of air transportation while supporting their Scope 3 decarbonisation goals through SAF environmental attributes.

text:
EVA Air has signed an MOU with freight forwarder AIT Worldwide Logistics to expand its Green Transportation Program over the next two years.

In year one, EVA Air will supply Microsoft with roughly 15,000 metric tonnes of CO₂e in Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF) environmental attributes, helping offset the Scope 3 emissions tied to air-freighting Microsoft's cloud infrastructure equipment.

Microsoft and Formosa Petrochemical Corporation (FPCC) also attended the signing ceremony, demonstrating a shared goal across the aviation, energy, logistics and technology sectors to accelerate lower-carbon air transportation.

A Taiwan-based fuel supply chain

In this collaboration, the flights will depart from Taiwan using SAF supplied by FPCC. Produced from used cooking oil (UCO), the fuel has been certified under the International Sustainability and Carbon Certification (ISCC) system for both its feedstock and production process.

"Achieving net-zero aviation requires collaboration across the entire value chain, from airlines and fuel suppliers to logistics providers and corporate customers," says Clay Sun, President of EVA Air.

"This collaboration demonstrates that when customer demand is aligned with industry resources, it can accelerate the development of the SAF market. We look forward to working with more partners to make lower-carbon air transportation the new standard for global supply chains."

In comparison to conventional jet fuel, SAF delivers approximately 80% lower lifecycle greenhouse gas emissions. The associated SAF environmental attributes will be issued and retired through the ISCC Credit Transfer System (CTS), an internationally recognised registry for tracking sustainability attributes, enabling Microsoft to account for the resulting Scope 3 emissions reductions associated with air freight transportation.

Supporting Microsoft's carbon-negative goal

This will help to drive Microsoft's sustainability efforts. In 2020, it committed to being carbon negative by 2030. As it looks to advance this ambition, Microsoft has worked to invest in SAF as well as other solutions to help drive emissions reduction through the value chain.

This partnership showcases how investment like this, alongside corporate demand, accelerates SAF adoption while also aiding the expansion of Taiwan's domestic SAF market and a broader low-carbon aviation ecosystem.

Scaling a repeatable model

Around the world, demand for lower-carbon supply chains and sustainable transportation continues to grow, and EVA Air has been actively expanding its SAF strategy.

Since 2025, the airline has regularly incorporated SAF into flights departing from Asia, Europe and North America, while also signing a five-year SAF procurement agreement with FPCC.

Through its Green Transportation Program, EVA Air helps corporate customers and freight forwarders better understand the carbon footprint of air transportation while supporting their Scope 3 decarbonisation goals through SAF environmental attributes.

Together with AIT, Microsoft and FPCC, EVA Air aims to establish a scalable and repeatable collaboration model that encourages broader corporate participation, expands SAF adoption and accelerates aviation's transition toward net zero.

"Every year, our teams are shipping large volumes of sensitive, high-value air cargo from Taiwan. EVA Air has been the partner of choice to support our exponential growth in the region and our trust in their executive leadership is rooted in decades-long relationships," AIT's Chief Strategy Officer, Greg Weigel, adds.

"By demonstrating the benefits of this collaboration with Microsoft, a strategically important customer; EVA Air, one of our core carriers; and FPCC, a local SAF producer, we hope to influence the market and inspire similar collaborations between airlines, producers, forwarders and customers in the Asia-Pacific region."

EVA Air's Chief Sustainability Officer Jason Liu and AIT Worldwide Logistics' Chief Strategy Officer Greg Weigel put pen to paper on the MOU, with the signing witnessed by a cross-section of senior figures: Taiwan Civil Aviation Administration Director General Shu-Ping Ho, American Institute in Taiwan Commercial Section Deputy Chief Eric Crowley, EVA Air President Clay Sun, FPCC President Keh-Yen Lin, AIT Executive Vice President of Global Operations Ryan Carter and Vincent Shih, General Manager of Corporate, External, and Legal Affairs for Microsoft Taiwan.

Between them, the four organisations now cover the full SAF value chain, from fuel production and aviation through to logistics and end corporate customers, pushing supply chain decarbonisation and aviation's low-carbon transition further forward.

A growing sustainability track record

The agreement adds to EVA Air's broader push on sustainability governance and disclosure.

The carrier has taken part in the S&P Global Corporate Sustainability Assessment (CSA) since 2021 and has earned a place in The Sustainability Yearbook for five years running. It also became the sole Taiwanese airline named to the Dow Jones Best-in-Class Emerging Markets Index (DJBIC) in May 2026.

The DJBIC ranks among the foremost global sustainability benchmarks, assessing companies on environmental, social, governance and economic performance using S&P Global's CSA methodology, a further mark of EVA Air's progress on governance and decarbonisation.

The airline says it will keep scaling up SAF use, sharpening operational efficiency and deepening ties with suppliers, corporate customers and global partners as it works toward net-zero aviation and sustainable long-term growth.

text:
Formosa Plastics New Smart, a subsidiary of the Formosa Plastics Group (1301.TW), announced today (27th) that its affiliate Chenghao Technology has officially obtained ISCC EU international sustainability and carbon certification for its algae oil technology development, establishing a critical foundation for algae oil to enter the international sustainable fuel supply chain and marking a breakthrough in the key verification mechanism for renewable fuel feedstock to enter the European sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) supply chain.

With the Taiwanese government setting a policy target of 5% SAF usage for Taiwanese airlines by 2030, Formosa Plastics New Smart is developing Taiwanese-made emerging feedstock through microalgae, aiming to enhance the stability and self-reliance of aviation green energy. Wang Jui-yu, Chairwoman of both Formosa Plastics New Smart and Formosa Plastics Biomedical, stated that in response to future SAF demand growth, feedstock supply must develop along multiple pathways. Formosa Plastics Biomedical will start from circular economy principles, recycling waste cooking oil to refine into SAF feedstock; Formosa Plastics New Smart will develop locally producible bio-based feedstock through microalgae technology. These two pathways—one leveraging existing resource recycling and the other pioneering emerging bio-based technology—each offer distinct advantages and complement one another.

She noted that only through diversified parallel approaches can Taiwan build a self-reliant and resilient next-generation SAF feedstock supply system. ISCC EU is a sustainability certification scheme recognized by the European Union. The certification scope covers microalgae cultivation and algae oil production, and also includes greenhouse gas emissions calculation and related management mechanism verification, extending algae oil development from the technical level to compliance with international sustainability standards. The company will subsequently advance process scale-up, production efficiency improvement, and cost optimization, moving from pilot production to mid-scale and commercial-scale validation.

Liu Hui-chi, General Manager of Formosa Plastics New Smart, explained from a technical perspective that the key to microalgae truly advancing toward SAF applications lies in oil production efficiency, process stability, and scalability. Chenghao has developed high-efficiency oil-producing algae strains and heterotrophic fermentation mass production technology. Through proprietary cultivation conditions and industrial-grade modular design, the algae biomass oil content can reach 50% to 60%. The current 500-liter pilot production line has completed phased mass production formulation and stability assessments, and the algae oil produced meets downstream refining feedstock specifications, demonstrating that the technology has progressed from the R&D stage to possessing a practical foundation for actual SAF refining applications.

The international certification was audited by Bureau Veritas (BV) as the third-party verifier. Hsu Pei-shih, BV's Deputy General Manager, stated that Chenghao's achievement of ISCC EU certification demonstrates its solid results in algae oil technology development and sustainability management, reflecting Formosa Plastics New Smart's proactive positioning in advancing the industrialization of emerging bio-based feedstock and its continued alignment with international standards.

Formosa Plastics New Smart indicated that it will continue to leverage the Formosa Plastics Group's industrial resources to advance microalgae technology scale-up and algae oil industrialization, strengthen the connection from technology development to market application, expand the commercialization of emerging bio-based feedstock, and provide more diversified options for aviation's net-zero transition.

The Formosa Plastics Group's dual-track strategy in the SAF sector is gradually taking shape. Formosa Plastics Biomedical focuses on waste cooking oil recycling and reuse, representing the existing resource circularity pathway; Formosa Plastics New Smart is investing in microalgae cultivation and algae oil production, representing the pioneering of emerging bio-based technology. Although the two take different technical routes, both point toward the same goal: building localized feedstock supply capabilities in Taiwan amid clear SAF policy demand and intensifying international decarbonization pressure.

Industry analysts note that SAF is regarded as one of the key solutions for the aviation industry to achieve net-zero emissions, but current global SAF production capacity remains far below demand, making feedstock acquisition a priority for countries worldwide. Taiwan's aviation fuel is almost entirely import-dependent. If Taiwan can establish a self-reliant supply chain through Taiwanese-made feedstock such as microalgae, it would not only reduce external dependence but also potentially gain a first-mover advantage in the Asia-Pacific green aviation fuel market.

From a technical process perspective, Chenghao's algae oil has advanced from laboratory R&D to the 500-liter pilot production stage, with oil content of 50% to 60% representing a competitive level in the bio-based feedstock sector. However, there remains some distance from commercial-scale production, and subsequent mid-scale and commercial-scale validation will be key areas to watch. Market observers point out that the challenge in biofuel industrialization often lies not in the technology itself, but in whether production costs after scale-up can compete with conventional aviation fuel and imported SAF—a critical issue that Formosa Plastics New Smart must address going forward.

text:
The White House has asked federal environmental regulators to allow the nation’s small oil refineries to blend less biofuels into their gasoline and diesel than initially projected as part of the administration’s efforts to ease pump prices, according to two administration officials.

Such an outcome would please the oil industry, but trigger a backlash in the Midwest where agricultural interests have fought ferociously for strong biofuel mandates to support the country's farmers.

Under federal law, refiners are required to blend tens of billions of gallons of biofuels like corn-based ethanol into the country’s fuel pool or buy renewable blending credits, called RINs, from those that do. Each gallon of biofuel produced generates RINs. But smaller plants can apply for waivers if they demonstrate the requirements put them in financial hardship.

The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) is reviewing 34 such requests and has projected approving enough waivers to cover around a billion RINs of biofuel blending obligations this year. A decision, the EPA said on Friday, is expected by the end of this month.

The White House has asked the EPA in recent meetings, however, to waive a higher volume than that, the two sources told Reuters, asking not to be named. The push is being driven by senior White House adviser Stephen Miller, members of the administration's Energy Dominance Council and other policy advisers concerned about high energy costs, the sources said.

Several oil and biofuel industry representatives briefed by the administration on the matter told Reuters they expected the EPA to ultimately approve anywhere between 1.2 and 1.8 billion RINs in Small Refinery Exemptions.

That would cut meaningfully into overall biofuel blending mandates for the year, which the EPA had set at a record 26.81 billion RINs for 2026.

The EPA told Reuters that it is not being directed by the White House on which waiver requests should be approved or denied, and added that no decisions have yet been made.

Representatives of Stephen Miller did not respond to a request for comment. The White House, which encompasses the Energy Dominance Council, deferred comments to the EPA.

The issue revives one of the most contentious battles from the first Trump administration when the EPA significantly expanded the exemption program to assuage the refining industry, but angered the Farm Belt in the meantime.

POLITICAL CALCULATION

The push from top Trump administration officials to expand the program reflects rising concerns about high gasoline prices since the U.S. conflict with Iran interrupted Middle East oil exports through the Strait of Hormuz. Those pump prices are a potential liability for Trump's fellow Republicans leading into the November midterm elections.

Refiners argue that high biofuel blending obligations raise the price of gasoline by imposing higher operating costs. But biofuel advocates reject that argument and say ethanol lowers fuel prices by pumping up supply volumes with a relatively cheap additive.

The Trump administration has already made several other moves to reduce energy costs, including releasing emergency oil stockpiles and waiving certain anti-smog regulations for gasoline during summer months, but fuel prices remain stubbornly above $4 a gallon.

The question of expanded biofuel waivers has already raised the hackles of agricultural backers in the Farm Belt eager to get ahead of the EPA decision.

On Tuesday, the attorneys general of Iowa, South Dakota and Missouri sent a letter to EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin urging him to reject broad refinery waiver requests, arguing that recent glowing refining industry earnings reports undermine claims that refiners are suffering economic hardship.

"The refineries want to have their cake and eat it, too," the letter said.

Senator Chuck Grassley of Iowa said on X on Monday: "I sure hope the Trump admin won’t give small refinery exemptions at a near record level. Would only help petroleum refiners making record profits."

The prospect of large-scale exemptions, meanwhile, has already hit RIN prices, which plunged to their lowest level in more than four months on Monday.

The American Soybean Association said high exemptions could eliminate around 500 million gallons of biodiesel and renewable diesel demand and cost soybean farmers about $1 billion in lost revenue.

text:
Navigating book-and-claim instruments and Scope 3 flexibility credibly, under the new Corporate Net-Zero Standard.

For most companies, the emissions that matter most sit outside their own operations — in the electricity grid, in supply chains, in the fuel burned by planes they’ve never chartered. Energy Attribute Certificates, Sustainable Aviation Fuel certificates, and carbon credits all exist to let organisations claim progress on exactly this kind of emissions they don’t physically control. The question is no longer whether these instruments are allowed — SBTi’s Corporate Net-Zero Standard V2.0 has explicitly opened the door to them through new “activity pools” for Scope 3. It’s whether your approach would hold up under real scrutiny.

Join Anthesis for a practical, in-person breakfast session on what these instruments actually are, where they overlap and where they don’t, and how to build a defensible claims strategy rather than a collection of certificates bought to fill a gap.

Why now?

SBTi’s Corporate Net-Zero Standard V2.0 has introduced more flexibility for Scope 3 target-setting, including activity pools that allow companies to count certain market-based instruments (like EACs and SAF certificates) toward their reduction claims. That’s welcome news for companies with limited supply chain leverage. But it also raises the bar: stakeholders are increasingly asking, not just “do you have certificates?” but “are they additional, are they high-quality, and do they actually represent the claim you’re making?”

If your organisation is buying renewable energy certificates, exploring SAF as part of a corporate travel or logistics footprint, or relying on carbon credits to bridge the gap to your target, it’s worth asking: do you understand what each instrument actually proves? Could you defend your claims stack to a sceptical stakeholder? And is it built to hold up as SBTi’s rules and market expectations keep evolving?

text:
Fuel Initiative Boosts Defence Resilience

(Australian Government Defence) The Australian Defence Force has begun rolling out low carbon liquid fuel (LCLF) blends across its network in an effort to strengthen fuel resilience.

The initiative introduces aviation and diesel fuels containing synthetic components to fuel installations nationwide and aligns with the 2026 National Defence Strategy to enhance energy security and operational readiness.

According to Director General Fuel Capability Brigadier Mark Baldock, diversifying fuel sources is essential to enhancing Defence’s energy security.

“Supporting domestic renewable fuel production strengthens Australia’s sovereign capability. These demonstrations are an important step toward building a more resilient and sustainable energy future for Defence,” Brigadier Baldock said.

Policy adviser from the Defence Energy Transition Office (DETO) Commander Steve Cole said it was inevitable that Defence would start to use LCLF.

“Australia is increasingly looking to be self-sufficient, so the focus at DETO is making sure that Defence is prepared to use these fuels as they become available,” Commander Cole said.

Low carbon liquid fuels are made from a source other than crude oil – be it canola oil, sugar cane, waste oils or forestry residue.

'These demonstrations are an important step toward building a more resilient and sustainable energy future for Defence.'

They are chemically indistinguishable from fossil fuels, allowing them to be used without modifications to ADF equipment.

DETO has undertaken certification processes and platform demonstrations of renewable diesel and sustainable aviation fuels, including during Exercise Talisman Sabre and the Avalon Air Show.

“A big part of these demonstrations has been taking maintainers and crews of the platforms, planners and decision-makers on a journey to understand we are talking about drop-in replacement fuels that meet the same specifications,” Commander Cole said.

Since then, DETO has focused on adopting certification for ADF platforms to ensure internal assurance processes are met and to facilitate interoperability with partner nations that are also adopting LCLFs.

All ADF aviation and land assets are now certified to operate on LCLF, with RAAF Base East Sale and the Army Aviation Training Centre already using blended fuel. Certification of remaining maritime platforms is nearing completion.

Defence has established the Defence Fuels Qualification Centre in partnership with the Defence Science and Technology Group.

title: Massive refinery exemptions would undo progress under Trump's 2026-2027 RFS blending levels
description:
Such an action would undermine the progress made since President Trump finalized record RFS blending levels in March, according to a press release.
“President Trump rightly garnered much praise in March by finalizing the most robust RFS blending levels in history,” said Monte Shaw, Executive Director of the Iowa Renewable Fuels Association.
“To reverse course now by granting massive levels of unjustified refinery exemptions would be bad policy, bad economics, and bad for farmers.
So-called record-breaking RFS levels don’t mean a thing if they are reversed through unjustified refinery exemptions.
“Since President Trump put the RFS back on track in March, it has been doing exactly what it was supposed to – driving demand for biofuels.
text:
WEST DES MOINES, IA: This week biofuels markets have been thrown into chaos over rumors that the EPA may grant nearly double the forecasted amount of refinery exemptions (SREs) from the 2025 Renewable Fuel Standard (RFS) blending levels. In March, the EPA forecasted less than one billion gallons of exemptions for 2025, but now it now has been reported the agency plans to exempt 1.8 billion gallons. Such an action would undermine the progress made since President Trump finalized record RFS blending levels in March, according to a press release.

“President Trump rightly garnered much praise in March by finalizing the most robust RFS blending levels in history,” said Monte Shaw, Executive Director of the Iowa Renewable Fuels Association. “To reverse course now by granting massive levels of unjustified refinery exemptions would be bad policy, bad economics, and bad for farmers. We are hoping this is just another false rumor floated in the media to roil the markets so some credit trader can try to make a buck. But if there is substance behind the rumors, it is not too late to change course and to commit to a robust RFS – a commitment President Trump made in March, a commitment that is working, and a commitment that EPA should not undermine.”

In March, EPA announced that it would clear a backlog of refinery exemption requests from the previous administration covering the 2023-2025 compliance years. The agency adopted a Dept. of Energy methodology to evaluate the requests. In order to minimize the damage to renewable fuel producers, the EPA agreed to reallocate 70% of the exemptions to the remaining obligated parties. At that time, renewable fuels supporters argued for 100% reallocation and few, if any, refiner exemptions. However, combined with record-breaking RFS blend levels for 2026-2027, most biofuels supporters remained generally positive.

“If a new methodology is adopted that grants nearly all refinery exemption requests for the 2025 compliance year, that would equate to roughly one billion lost biofuel gallons,” said Shaw. “And the damage wouldn’t stop there. Applied to 2026-2027, it would mean nearly a billion lost gallons each year going forward as well. So-called record-breaking RFS levels don’t mean a thing if they are reversed through unjustified refinery exemptions. IRFA members urge President Trump to throw this rumor on the ash heap of history, to stand by his commitment to American farmers, and to order the EPA to deny the baseless claims of economic harm by some refiners at a time of record refinery profits.”

Since the EPA finalized the RFS blending levels for 2026-2027 in March, there has been a strong resurgence of biodiesel production in Iowa and around the country, with record production during the last few months. The strong RFS rule that Trump finalized was having an undeniably positive impact.

“Since President Trump put the RFS back on track in March, it has been doing exactly what it was supposed to – driving demand for biofuels. Both biodiesel and ethanol demand hit records this year. In Iowa, we had biodiesel plants that were shuttered or running at very reduced rates. Today they are producing at full capacity, buying soybean oil from our farmers, and hiring back workers that had been let go. It would be reckless and almost unimaginable to pull the rug out from under this success story at the request of a handful of oil refiners that are certainly not suffering from economic hardship during this time of high oil and fuel prices.”

title: Tsinghua achieves world-first direct CO₂-to-SAF conversion at kiloton scale | EurekAlert!
description:
Batteries are still too heavy for long-haul flights, and today’s “green” jet fuels rely on scarce used cooking oil and crops that compete with food supplies.
Now, a team at Tsinghua University has demonstrated a fundamentally different path: making certified jet fuel directly from industrial CO₂ and green hydrogen, at the thousand-ton scale.

text:
BEIJING, August 17, 2026 — Aviation is one of the last great frontiers of decarbonization. Batteries are still too heavy for long-haul flights, and today’s “green” jet fuels rely on scarce used cooking oil and crops that compete with food supplies. Now, a team at Tsinghua University has demonstrated a fundamentally different path: making certified jet fuel directly from industrial CO₂ and green hydrogen, at the thousand-ton scale.

On August 17, 2026, the China Petroleum and Chemical Industry Federation (CPCIF) convened an expert panel in Beijing to evaluate the “Kiloton-Scale CO₂ Hydrogenation to Sustainable Aviation Fuel” technology. The panel concluded that the achievement, led by Professor Fei Wei and Associate Professor Chenxi Zhang of the Department of Chemical Engineering, is world-first and internationally leading overall.

From Smokestack to Sky

Unlike conventional SAF routes that face hard feedstock limits, CO₂AF™ uses two inputs with no practical ceiling: captured industrial CO₂ and green hydrogen from wind and solar power. Inside a purpose-built high-pressure reactor, a uniquely designed catalyst performs in a single step what previously required complex, multi-stage refineries—rearranging CO₂ and hydrogen molecules into liquid hydrocarbons indistinguishable from conventional jet fuel.

Associate Professor Chenxi Zhang calls this “artificial photosynthesis.” Just as plants use sunlight to turn CO₂ into glucose, CO₂AF™ uses green hydrogen and advanced catalysts to turn CO₂ into liquid fuel, releasing only water. The carbon is borrowed, not mined: captured from emissions, flown across the sky, and ready to be captured again.

The Numbers That Matter

During a rigorous 72-hour continuous test at the pilot plant in Meishan, Sichuan Province, independent experts verified:

97.37% of the CO₂ fed into the system was converted into products

92.37% of the output was premium C₈⁺ aviation fuel range hydrocarbons

1.67% was methane byproduct—meaning nearly every carbon atom became useful fuel, not waste

The reactor ran at 100.01% of design capacity, with internal temperatures stable within ±2.3°C

The final product met all specifications of GB 6537-2025, China’s standard for No. 3 Jet Fuel. It is a true “drop-in” fuel: zero engine modifications, zero infrastructure changes. Notably, unlike many existing SAFs that are paraffin-based, CO₂AF™ produces a full-range aromatic fuel—matching the complete molecular profile of conventional petroleum jet fuel.

Breaking the Old Limits

For decades, CO₂-to-fuel research hit three walls. Thermodynamically, CO₂ is stubbornly stable. Kinetically, pushing conversion high usually destroyed selectivity—turning precious fuel into useless methane. Economically, complex multi-step processes consumed too much energy and hydrogen.

CO₂AF™ appears to have cracked all three. By comparison, the conventional Fischer-Tropsch route is theoretically capped below 50% selectivity for aviation-range fuels. The dominant HEFA process (used cooking oil) is already bumping against global supply limits. CO₂AF™ leapfrogs both, achieving over 92% selectivity in one step from feedstocks that are, for all practical purposes, unlimited.

What the Experts Said

“This is not merely an incremental improvement—it is a fundamentally new route,” the evaluation panel wrote in its official conclusion. “By establishing a new paradigm of catalytic nano-reconstruction and solving the autonomous design and manufacturing challenges of high-pressure fluidized-bed reactors, this technology offers a Chinese solution to global aviation decarbonization.”

From Laboratory to Industry

The technology has already traveled from lab bench to industrial pilot. Since its transfer from Tsinghua University in 2022, the Sichuan plant has logged over 2,000 hours of operation. The team is now engineering a 50,000-ton commercial demonstration plant in Ordos, Inner Mongolia, designed to pair with local renewable energy for fully green hydrogen production.

Experts recommend accelerating this scale-up and integrating CO₂AF™ into international certification frameworks such as ASTM D7566 and China’s CAAC SAF standards.

The Bottom Line

As nations worldwide mandate ever-higher SAF blending quotas, the world faces a supply crunch. CO₂AF™ does not ask farmers for more crops or restaurants for more grease. It asks smokestacks for the CO₂ they were going to emit anyway.

title: Air France Just Made Its Cheapest Awards Worse—My Plan To Beat The Devaluation And ...
description:
Air France KLM Flying Blue is making its cheapest awards worse beginning September 8.
Why I Actually Want Flying Blue Platinum The latest Frequent Miler On The Air does an excellent job laying out shortcuts to Flying Blue status.
You’ll often see 60,000 miles in business class when members without status see 142,000 miles or more.
Flying Blue Status Is Stupidly Complex I genuinely don’t know how the median Frenchman could possibly figure this out?
Bilt Platinum members get 12 months of Flying Blue Gold after transferring 10,000 Bilt points to Flying Blue.
text:
Air France KLM Flying Blue is making its cheapest awards worse beginning September 8. The lowest-priced awards will become “Light” fares: no changes, no refunds, fewer checked bags, paid advance seat assignments and, remarkably, no lounge access even when redeeming for business class.

You can pay more miles for a Standard award that restores most of what the same number of miles buys today, or still more for a Flex award. In Flying Blue’s New York – Paris business class example:

Light costs 60,000 miles plus $608.83.

Standard costs 75,000 miles plus $608.83.

Flex costs 110,000 miles plus $302.82.

So this is effectively a 25% increase if you want today’s ordinary award benefits. One importance nuance though is that elite benefits still apply to Light awards. Silver restores baggage and seat selection benefits. Gold restores lounge access. Platinum also provides free award changes and refunds. That turns elite status into a way of opting out of most of the devaluation.

I already have Flying Blue Gold through a Bilt status match. Now I plan to pursue Platinum because of two additional benefits.

Why I Actually Want Flying Blue Platinum

The latest Frequent Miler On The Air does an excellent job laying out shortcuts to Flying Blue status. Gold has already been useful to me for priority boarding, free checked bags and free exit row seats when flying Delta. Platinum adds more baggage, free award changes and refunds. But the two things I care about are:

Better award availability. The difference in saver award space is significant. You’ll often see 60,000 miles in business class when members without status see 142,000 miles or more. This matters even more when booking several seats for a family.

Ability to redeem for Air France La Première first class. These awards are still expensive and scarce. And they only allow one seat per flight currently. Ben Smith hates mileage redemption for first class. But it’s one of the world’s best overall passenger experiences, including the first class lounge in Paris.

Under the new system, Platinum can book the cheapest Light award, receive status-based bags, seats and lounge access, and still change or cancel without charge. A 60,000 mile Light award effectively becomes a 110,000 mile Flex award (albeit with the standard cash surcharge). And it has better availability. And I can book first class.

Flying Blue Status Is Stupidly Complex

I genuinely don’t know how the median Frenchman could possibly figure this out? Flying Blue awards Experience Points, generally abbreviated as XP, toward status. Starting without status, you need:

100 XP for Silver;

then another 180 XP for Gold; and

then another 300 XP for Platinum.

Each threshold is deducted when you reach it and a new 12-month qualification period begins. You therefore need 580 XP to go from nothing to Platinum. You cannot simply earn 300 XP for Platinum.

But a status match changes the equation. Bilt Platinum members get 12 months of Flying Blue Gold after transferring 10,000 Bilt points to Flying Blue. You receive the 10,000 Flying Blue miles (it’s not a status fee). And while the partnership lasts, the benefit can be re-upped each year. Mine recently expired and I’m purposely waiting to re-up.

The match gives you gold. It doesn’t give you XP. But once you are Gold, Platinum is earned with 300 XP in the upcoming 12 months. Flying Blue has also has a paid status match to Gold for $199. With Flying Blue, timing is everything.

The Bank Of America Card Gets Me 260 Of The 300 XP

The $89-annual-fee Air France KLM Visa Signature Card, whose improved status-earning structure I explained earlier this year, currently offers 70,000 miles and 100 XP after $3,000 in purchases during the first 90 days. It also provides:

20 XP each account anniversary

an additional 80 XP at the anniversary after spending $15,000 during the card year, and

another 60 XP after spending $25,000 during the card year.

That is 160 anniversary XP after $25,000 in total spending (not $25,000 on top of the first $15,000). Combined with the 100 XP initial bonus offer, the card can produce 260 XP during its first year. Starting from matched Gold, that leaves just 40 XP for Platinum.

The card earns 3 miles per dollar on Air France KLM and SkyTeam airlines (Delta, i.e. earns more on Delta tickets than buying with a Delta card does) and dining, 3 miles per dollar on rent paid through Bilt up to $50,000 per year (for a fee), and 1.5 miles per dollar elsewhere. I can earn 2 transferable points per dollar on other cards, so there is a real opportunity cost to putting $25,000 here.

The Timing Trick That Makes This Work

If the 100-XP welcome bonus posts while I have no status, Flying Blue will use those points to grant Silver and deduct them from my account. They will no longer be available for the climb from Gold to Platinum.

But the 160 XP from annual spending doesn’t post as the spending occurs. It arrives at or shortly after the card anniversary. If I activate the Bilt Gold match before opening the card, the matched status can expire before those anniversary points arrive. Then they don’t help for Platinum. So the way to do this is:

Apply for the Bank of America card first.

Don’t immediately complete the initial bonus offer spending.

Wait ~ 60 to 75 days after opening the card before activating a new Bilt Gold match. (creating a buffer between the first card anniversary and the end of the matched qualification year, allowing time for the anniversary XP to post).

Once Flying Blue shows Gold again, finish the $3,000 spending requirement before day 90. (The 100 initial XP should hit my Gold account rather than being consumed to create Silver.)

Spend $25,000 total during the cardmember year. (The first $3,000 is included in that amount.)

Earn another 40 XP before the matched Gold qualification period closes.

Once the 160 anniversary XP arrives, I should have 300 XP and move to Platinum – but it’ll take about a year from the time I get approved for the card. That doesn’t hit when you reach $25,000 spend, but after your cardmember anniversary. So needlessly complicated.

How To Earn The Missing 40 XP

I have several options, and the best answer is to combine activities I would undertake anyway.

Credit paid SkyTeam flights to Flying Blue. XP depends upon cabin, distance band and segments rather than ticket price. Connections can be valuable, and short international business class flights are disproportionately rewarding. For example, a paid Delta first class roundtrip from Austin to Canada or Mexico via a U.S. hub should earn 42 XP: 6 XP for each domestic segment and 15 XP for each short international segment.

Link Flying Blue with Accor Live Limitless. I haven’t previously used the partnership bonus offer, so the first eligible Accor stay after linking earns 5 XP and the first eligible Air France or KLM flight earns another 5 XP.

Contribute toward sustainable aviation fuel. Flying Blue awards 1 XP for each €10 contributed on an eligible Air France or KLM booking. Forty XP therefore costs about €400, or €300 after collecting the 10 Accor XP. The XP posts after the flight departs, and the contribution can be attached to an award booking even though the award flight itself doesn’t earn XP.

Donate Flying Blue miles to charity. Every 2,000 miles donated earns 1 XP, credited immediately. Forty XP would require 80,000 miles. That is a terrible value compared with €400 of sustainable fuel, but useful on an emergency basis right before a qualification deadline.

Buy an Air France Discount Pass. A new subscription or renewal comes with 20 XP and 2,500 or 5,000 miles. This is not cheaper than buying sustainable fuel solely for XP, but it can make sense for someone who will use the pass benefits.

Can I Reach Platinum Without Waiting A Year?

The frustrating part of this plan is waiting for the 160 card-spending XP to post at the first anniversary. Spending $25,000 quickly does not accelerate it. I’d probably do this with housing, quarterly tax or property tax payments (all of which come at a cost).

After receiving the 100 initial XP, I could reach Platinum earlier by producing the remaining 200 XP through paid flying, €2,000 of sustainable-fuel contributions, 400,000 donated miles, or some combination. Two well-routed paid business class trips between the United States and Europe with connecting segments can generate roughly 200 XP.

Another possibility raised by Frequent Miler is holding two Bank of America Flying Blue cards. If Bank of America approves two accounts and each awards the full anniversary XP, spending $25,000 on each would generate 320 XP annually, enough to maintain Platinum without flying. The terms limit a member to one new-account XP bonus every 24 months but appear to contemplate multiple accounts. I’d love to hear from readers that have tried this.

Generally you can open up to 2 BofA cards in 2 months, no more than in a year, and no more than 4 in two years. And they won’t usually approve cardmembers who have 3 or more new accounts open with any issuer in the past 12 months (though if you have a deposit account with them it’s 7 accounts in 12 months) however I’ve seen mixed data points on this guideline.

Earning Platinum Once Is Easier Than Keeping It

The first-year card bonus gets me to 260 XP. In subsequent years, one card provides only 160 XP after $25,000 in spending, leaving 140 XP per year to maintain Platinum.

That can come from paid flying, sustainable fuel contributions, a second card or a mixture. If I don’t requalify, Flying Blue provides a soft landing to Gold rather than dropping me to the bottom. Earning Platinum once therefore gives me a year of Platinum followed by at least a year of Gold, and potentially Silver after that. Ten consecutive years of Platinum earns Platinum for life.

I wouldn’t normally recommend chasing airline status for benefits that can be purchased more cheaply. I don’t value this for the checked bags and seat assignments and lounge access. I get those already. But savings on redemptions for my full family, which I’ll do with Air France at least once a year but given the savings it’s probably four seats times two trips.
